Hello team,

[~accountid:712020:ca818823-efac-45fe-ba7d-a6686a5e08b5] There are no strict requirements for the language of the T&Cs, but it would be preferable if they could be bilingual. It probably wouldn’t be too difficult to generate a translation with ChatGPT and then have a local colleague who speaks the language review it. We could also add a note at the end stating that, in case of any discrepancies between the two versions, the English version shall prevail.

My main concern is with the automatic opt-in in Norway and Finland. Therefore, to reduce the related risk, I propose the following:
1️⃣ Inform all eligible drivers before the campaign starts that they’ll be automatically included but can opt out anytime without consequences.
2️⃣ Provide an easy, no-friction opt-out (email to [giveaways@bolt.eu|mailto:giveaways@bolt.eu]) that takes effect immediately.
3️⃣ Keep all campaign messages purely informational — no ads or unrelated promotions.
4️⃣ Log proof that notices were sent and opt-outs handled — this makes automatic inclusion defensible under local law.

I believe the T&Cs should be publicly accessible, and the comms should include a clear link to where the T&Cs can be found - or ideally, the T&Cs could even be attached directly to the comms themselves.

Thanks!

Our  approach has been that output-based incentives (“Do X, get Y” — e.g. complete 50 deliveries in a week to earn an extra €100) are much safer than incentives tied to acceptance rate or online time (e.g. “stay online for three hours on Saturday”). From that perspective, the proposed campaign structure is acceptable. Although usually the timeframe for achieving the delivery target is longer (e.g. 1 week) so that couriers can realistically complete the required number of deliveries without having to remain online continuously. But I think this is a risk that is unavoidable here, as it’s targeted for a specific timeframe.I think what’s important here is that:

# the team avoids terms like “be online between 18-20” (which sounds like a required work period) and instead use “Complete 6+ deliveries between 17:00–19:00" - this implies that there’s an eligibility window for an output-based incentive. 
# The campaign is one-off and not continuous.

I haven’t seen other markets run campaigns that specifically target couriers who’ve been inactive during a particular day or time slot (like the past three Saturdays). In that sense, this setup is somewhat new.
 That said, I think it’s not fundamentally different from campaigns aimed at couriers inactive for a longer period (e.g. the past week), which imo are quite common (e.g. to win back churned to likely-to-churn couriers). The only difference is that this campaign uses a shorter inactivity window, which could slightly increase the perception of Bolt steering couriers’ working patterns- though I think the underlying risk remains in the same category.

Hi, good to hear from the Netherlands market! 

There are couple of aspects we need to discuss before you can proceed live with this category as it does indeed entail a lot of fraud risk. 

I’ll simply list our main points of concern here:

# How we can prevent fraud best in your market in this scenario?
## Suggesting we pre-authorize/book whenever we can the first hour/predicted payment(s) to ensure a working payment method. This does depend on user payment method as well. 
## Suggesting we add a capturing logic for payments to avoid pushing high user debt but to keep as much as we can from the pre-booked amounts. Here again, we are dependent on logic and possibilities: we can’t keep, for example, any amount we haven’t been able to pre-book.
# How we can limit fraud?
## Perhaps to limit the category only to trusted users and spenders?
## Perhaps limit the available payment methods?
## Perhaps to add a final limit to the possible destinations update (or maximum trip length)? Not to allow fully endless driving through destination updates. 
# How we can resolve fraud? ← *This may be even the most important aspect for our discussions*
## Are we covered in the local T&C to potentially protect Bolt in case of category abuse? Under which conditions?
## Setting up the monitoring and operational procedure to ‘save’ Bolt and action any intentional fraud scenarios
### The right to deduct ride fare due to fraud from the driver-partner (also before it is paid out)
### The right to limit access to this category for those not ‘qualifying’ due to fraud suspicion or history

You can also have a look here for more information: [https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/COMM/pages/6677627397/Fraud+and+Driver+by+Hour+Long+Duration+Limitless+Stops+Categories|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/COMM/pages/6677627397/Fraud+and+Driver+by+Hour+Long+Duration+Limitless+Stops+Categories|smart-link]

Hi,
Giulio del Balzo di Caprigliano has identified that there is a data protection / data privacy consideration for this piece of work. 

Please review the ticket and if needed, then please create a sub-ticket for the Privacy team.

+*BACKGROUND*+

* On 14 November, Privacy Team were alerted about launch of WfW in Germany ([+here+|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C0460RJ5QEP/p1761751268308059]).
** Dawit was looped into this in July, and according to Ops “_no concerns were expressed… In the launch confluence, there is not mention of a privacy team, thus this was not done yet_”.
*** Apparently this was not addressed with Legal via an SD ticket. It was addressed in meetings and via the above Slack channel.
** Dovile has expressed a willingness to give us time for review, which is good: “_if we need to push the pilot because of the need to check these things, I'll be happy to do so. We have been working on this internally for a while and my main priority is to do this in the best possible and compliant manner_”.
* Based on a quick skim of the channel:
** We are partnering with a Berlin fleet to launch WfW in Germany. For the pilot phase, it will be a new scheduled rides category ('G-Cars for Women').
** In Germany, driver licences and ID cards do not have gender listed on them. However, there is a gender field on *passports*.
*** In July, discussions were had ([+link+|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C0460RJ5QEP/p1753190288693159]) regarding introducing an additional layer of verification for riders - asking them to upload a copy of their passports. However, it was pointed out that not all riders will be carrying a passport. As such, it appears that scope was expanded to IDs as well (even though these do not have a gender field), although +*_this is not clear_*+. It was either that or not verify at all (i.e., IDs would primarily be a deterrent). Discussion then turned ([+here+|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C0460RJ5QEP/p1761751268308059]) to other means of checking gender, given that people are generally reluctant to share such sensitive documents. Ultimately, it sounds like we may be going with passports.

+*ANALYSIS*+

* See previous high-level analysis. Generally ok to launch from a privacy POV, even though the feature itself is problematic ✅ 
* There is also the issue of agreements with the fleet, but presumably this will be addressed as part of the wider T&Cs project ✅ 
** Ultimately (per [+LSS-56516+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-56516]), we do not need to implement full data sharing terms - better to wait for global T&Cs/DSA. Provided that any applicable terms clarify the parties as independent controllers responsible for their own compliance, then this should be enough.
* Main issue here is the *collection of passport*, which appears to be happening on the rider side. As such, this is the main issue to consider.
** Re local laws on processing ID docs - There are some specific laws on copying ID docs (e.g., [+ID Law+|https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/englisch_pauswg/englisch_pauswg.html#p0185]). Generally, it seems advisable to rely on user *consent* to do this (this should be fine, given that we would probably delete it upon receipt of a deletion request anyway), and not pass copies on to any third parties. Since consent can be withdrawn, it is advisable to make a note of the gender as part of manual review (in case deleted), and to honour consent withdrawals (users can then re-upload if needed) ⚠️
** Could be regarded as excessive unless absolutely necessary ⚠️  This will depend on whether other methods are available. We would need to be specific and clear on why we are asking the user for their passport, and what will be done with it. (We cannot practically ask riders to redact / cover up certain info).
** Retention of copies of ID could also be viewed as unjustified ⚠️ ideal approach would be to extract the gender field and delete the rest. If we keep it, it must be clearly marked as a copy.
** If we are checking the ID docs automatically, then there is a risk of both ADM and errors/inaccuracy (also if processing biometrics of facial imagery, then A9 risks) ⚠️

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Questions:
** Are we collecting passport of drivers in addition to riders? If not, what is being decided based on my advice from the current ticket?

I had a discussion with [~accountid:62615f256cb53d006a6a3fe1] back in May on this topic. We’re aligned that such payments are likely to fall within the scope of “consideration” for DAC7 purposes. The term “consideration” should be interpreted broadly - as any form of compensation paid or credited to the seller in connection with their relevant activity. EMTA have confirmed in the past that their interpretation of the term is broad also - anything goes. 

In that sense, it’s more prudent for us to report them, since any underreporting risk would sit with the platform, not the driver. And if the goal of DAC7 is to capture underreported income, these payments are exactly the type that could easily go unreported unless we include them. 

I see these payments as quite similar to bonuses drivers receive for reaching certain thresholds or targets, and therefore, it seems reasonable to treat them in the same way - assuming, of course, they are not refunded. 

If they are refunded in a different reportable period, we could in theory treat that as a reduction in the previously reported amount to “correct” any overstatement. 

Regarding equity investments and convertible loans - our initial view is that these would fall outside the scope of “consideration” since they relate to equity or financing rather than compensation - but I’d still like to review the agreements to confirm.

As for bank guarantees, this one is a bit trickier. If we end up paying the bank on behalf of the driver under a guarantee, that could be seen as a form of consideration too - similar in effect to a direct payment to the driver.

Our current custom linter only allows checking individual lines and other basic things. It doesn’t recognise resources so we can’t easily enforce for the {{pgp_key}} existence. Parsing resources would technically either involve writing our own HCL parser in python or trying to find an existing one, neither one is really worth the effort.

The summary of what we decided with Nicolai:

We could prohibit {{aws_iam_access_key}} entirely, however SRE cloud would like to use it with the {{pgp_key}} argument for SMTP credentials among some other things in the future, meaning this rule would need to be excludable, a feature that already exists in the linter. That means the 50 existing use cases of {{aws_iam_access_key}} could be excluded easily, also any new usages would probably just ignore the rule, making the linter rule pretty useless overall.

Overall conclusion for now is that we lack tools to implement this in a way that would improve much in a reasonable amount of time.

{quote}…

After investigating the matter, we can confirm that both XML response formats you have observed are valid and correct. The NAV (Hungarian Tax Authority) system sends responses according to different XSD schemas, and both namespace configurations are compliant with their specifications.



Technical Details



# Proxy Functionality: Our `action-szamla_agent_taxpayer` interface acts as a proxy service. We forward the response received from NAV to our clients without any modification to the XML content. The response you receive is exactly what NAV sends to us.



# Namespace Variations: The two different namespace attributions you've observed are both valid according to NAV's XSD schemas:

* Format 1: Root element with `ns2:` prefix and various namespace declarations

* Format 2: Root element without prefix, with different namespace prefix assignments



Both formats are semantically equivalent and contain the same data structure. The difference lies only in how  the XML namespaces are declared and prefixed.



# NAV Documentation: The official NAV documentation and XSD schemas are available at:

[https://onlineszamla.nav.gov.hu/dokumentaciok|https://onlineszamla.nav.gov.hu/dokumentaciok|smart-link] 



The schemas are provided in a ZIP file, and the `invoiceApi.xsd` contains the relevant schema definitions. However, the XSD specifications do not enforce a specific namespace prefix configuration, which allows for the variations you've observed.



Recommendation:



Since both response formats are valid and we cannot control which format NAV sends, *your system needs to handle both namespace configurations* when parsing the XML response. This is a standard requirement when working with XML that may have different namespace prefix assignments.{quote}

Hey team!
We received DLA’s advise regarding this topic. You can access the fill advise [here.|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1-W47HWsO789X4q4ssL3cfGuh949lwol9mw6JYtjtDaI/edit?tab=t.0]

The advise regarding the [+*Fleet Agreement Template*+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1InhsX52amlssUA8h8mpWwJwWAAZ3ADKPDej_U5gDYvA/edit?tab=t.0] is the following:

* *Clause 2.1.:* eliminate “and its reliability”.
*REGIONAL LEGAL COMMENT:* we think this is acceptable and already made an edit suggestion in the template removing that wording.

* *Clause 2.1.4.:* _Tracking the acceptance rate of each individual courier within the Fleet suggests an element of individual control over their performance, which should be avoided. Such monitoring has been interpreted as an indicator of the existence of a relationship of subordination, thereby increasing the risk of misclassification. It would be preferable to assess performance based only on the average acceptance rate across the Fleet._
*REGIONAL LEGAL COMMENT:* We are fully aligned with this understanding and therefore *strongly advise the team to not keep* the _“[4-week] Acceptance rate of Orders: ≥ 35[●]% [acceptance rate at the Fleet level] [acceptance rate by each authorised person in the Fleet]”_ KPI.
Since DLA did not raised any objection on the proposal of providing for parameters that refer to “Contact frequency” or even engagement, provided that they are linked to the Fleet and not individual couriers, with which we are aligned with, our proposal is that previous 2.1.4. is replaced by the following wording: _“[4 week] Engagement: ≥ [●] daily/weekly average number of logins and interactions of the Fleet with the BBB Platform, calculated on an aggregate basis”._
We already made an edit suggestion in the Template according to this.

* *Clause 2.2.:* _Please note that allowing the platform to unilaterally amend the standards or KPIs increases the risk of misclassification, as it demonstrates that these parameters are, in reality, set unilaterally by Bolt rather than being agreed with the Fleet. Ideally, any amendments to the standards should be mutually agreed between Bolt and the Fleet(s)._
*REGIONAL LEGAL COMMENT:* we understand DLA’s concern here and are aligned with their view. However, we believe that it is up for the Business to decide if we want to keep this or not. 

* *Clause 2.4.*: _This should be aligned with the General Terms. Also, it should be confirmed whether notice should, in this case, be granted and the clause should be adopted accordingly to reflect this decision._ 
*REGIONAL LEGAL COMMENT:* we are prepared to defend that this can be kept and does not require further changes in the General T&Cs, since it is not a general approach (at least for now), and it is only applicable to the Fleets with whom we enter the Fleet Agreements.


In conclusion, the [Fleet Agreement template |https://docs.google.com/document/d/1InhsX52amlssUA8h8mpWwJwWAAZ3ADKPDej_U5gDYvA/edit?tab=t.0]already has our edits suggestions, except for clause 2.2., which is for the Business to decide if it should be kept or not.


On the +*documentation topic*+ *, DLA advise is to have this topic addressed in the General T&Cs and not in the Fleet Agreements,* since “_This is not related to the Fleet’s performance”._ However, they do said that “_either option increases legal risk; it is more a matter of consistency”._

All questions related to the documentation topic were properly addressed and you can see the responses provided in t[he document. |https://docs.google.com/document/d/1-W47HWsO789X4q4ssL3cfGuh949lwol9mw6JYtjtDaI/edit?tab=t.0] We believe that for now in this ticket we should only focus on the question on weather this should be included in the Fleet Agreements or not.

Legal view is that this should be balanced with the possibility of loosing supply because of the fact that we demand a lot of documentation.
We are aligned with DLA’s view in including these concerns in the General T&Cs, since in this case:

* We can have something to show in case someone calls Bolt out for allowing couriers with an ilegal status to work with the Platform;
* If kept in the general T&Cs, it is going to be up to the team to decide if we really want to put these demands in practice.

Again, we believe that t*his is up for the business to decide* (if we want to address this in the General T&Cs or in the Fleet Agreements), but we should be aware that these obligations can lead to supply loss.

Please let us know if this should be added in the Fleet Agreement template.

Thank you!

Hey Team,

I reviewed the Auchan Retail Portugal (ARP) NDA against our playbook. Below are the must-have changes and the reason each is needed. I also introduced them and other edits in the [Gdoc|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1OftpCeJeFF2_AzCnl5v3H6gydwVyVVz3UDFKNyFLx-E/edit?tab=t.0] [~accountid:5b8d306bfa38ae2c89608b95] started working on as edits suggestions. If these are accepted, the NDA is fine to sign.

*Must-have changes (blockers)*

# Mutuality (protect both parties’ info)
*Issue:* NDA protects only ARP’s information.
*Change:* Make the definition/scope bilateral.
*Why:* Ensures our pricing, proposals, and methods are equally protected.

# Permitted disclosures & IT operations (staff/advisers/affiliates + backups)
*Issue:* Current clause prohibits even “arquivar”, which could block normal storage/backups and working with advisers.
*Change:* Add a standard permitted-disclosure and storage carve-out.
*Why:* Lets us operate normally without breaching the NDA.

# Survival tail
*Issue:* Duties end with the negotiations/contract; no post-term protection.
*Change:* Add a survival period.
*Why:* Standard market protection; aligns with our practice (I wrote 3 years, but we can go up to 5 years).

# Liability cap & indirects exclusion
*Issue:* Unlimited, vicarious exposure for any losses.
*Change:* Cap liability and limit to direct loss from breach of the NDA; exclude indirect/consequential loss.
*Proposed text:*
*Why:* Proportionate to an NDA; prevents open-ended risk (I kept the cap open, so you can tell me what do you think it is proportionate to this relationship/negotiations/future contracts).

# IP/ownership clarity
*Issue:* Clause implies all Confidential Information is ARP’s property.
*Change:* Preserve each party’s pre-existing IP and limit any license to evaluation.
*Why:* Protects our proposals and know-how from being treated as ARP property.

# Compelled disclosure notice
*Issue:* Legal-demand carve-out is vague.
*Change:* Specify timing and cooperation (2 days notice).
*Why:* Ensures we can seek protective measures.

These recommendations are the standard Bolt playbook positions for NDAs.

I do not think they will constitute a problem on Auchan’s end, because we are mainly making this mutual (which is standard practice) and aligning other things that were missing in their version.

My advise is for you to try to share this version with them and say that this is what we can accept.

Please do let me know if something else is needed!

Thank you!

h1. *Onboarding feedback* 

*Cognitive overload* 

Request to be mindful of cognitive load across the onboarding schedule, with particular emphasis on day 5, which contains: Building Blocks for Written Support, Building Blocks for Phone Support, Klaus and Quality Scorecard. 

* Solution: 
** Integrated mandatory break-time in the middle of the day (incorporated in the [newly proposed onboarding schedule|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1bSY4MrylPuCRsozC9v3Us9OcU2IsFWvmujexCnh0BiY/edit?gid=1011825742#gid=1011825742]) 
** Broke up concepts over two learning days

*Practice time* 

Highlighted that there was not enough time dedicated to actual Micromobility support-related tasks and topics. Request for an additional 2 days to focus on support and process-related scenarios and workshops. 

* Solution
** Added a day dedicated to case study work 
** Will refresh and expand on the _Common Support Issues_ section 
** We’ll also, as Trainers, work on building _scenario-based examples_ that will be integrated into facilitated sessions 

Add more examples of edge cases or how to handle more complex cases

* Solution 
** Can work some of these into scenario-based training tasks 

*Safety-related feedback*

* TP AZ: Requested to remove the Safety topic altogether from the onboarding process to instead introduce the subject in a learning plan a little while after new joiners begin to grasp concepts 
* TP NG: Requested for a more comprehensive Safety training as part of the onboarding process. 
** Will most likely share information about Micromobility Up-skill (can do this via _Learning Plans_) 
* "I think what I missed the most in the MM training were the topics related to Safety and Tier 2 collaboration. For example, when an accident happens, the case is handled by the Safety team, but often they can’t locate the trip, so they forward it to Tier 2 to try to find it. In the beginning, I had some difficulty locating these trips, and that part wasn’t covered in the training.
* Requests from Insurance Companies are another challenge. Many times, the case comes directly from the insurer rather than from any of the users involved in the accident, and they usually ask for information like the user’s name or contact details of the parties involved. These types of cases also weren’t included in the training.
* On top of that, the Safety team in MM can be quite difficult to deal with. So when a case comes from an Insurance Company, 200% of the time it has already been poorly handled beforehand, which makes it even harder to investigate. If the case had been properly logged in the Safety Tool, the insurer would already have all the details of the parties involved. However, in many situations, one of the people involved in the accident contacts the insurer directly, who then reaches out to us — and that’s when we realize the case was never logged as a Safety issue in the first place. Because of that, we don’t have the Insurance Claim document, which is essential for the insurer’s investigation to determine coverage.
* In short, these are the kinds of cases where we end up piecing things together from multiple sources to figure out where the process went wrong.

*General material upkeep* 

* Request to rework and beef up information in the sections covering internal tools (most likely related to _Admin for Micromobility_) 
* Some points are outdated, which complicates facilitated sessions - request to check that all sessions are true to current processes  
* Check simulators - some users tend to get stuck in some sections, and there are places where the clicking guidelines aren’t consistent. “Adding tips or best practices could make the training smoother and help learners navigate the system more efficiently.” 

*Out of scope*

* Providing visual guides or handouts of key information from the Onboarding program

Re the output: there are 3 huge contextual pieces to help understand the drivers of Timing CSAT. 

* Operations' health (more on-time orders lead to lower CSAT).
* Agent / AI efficiency. Timing tickets have a *63%* reopen rate (vs 37% for all Baltics tickets). The CSAT drop is 25 points for a reopened case.
* Process adherence.
** we’re only refunding 65% of cases where the policy allows us to refund. The CSAT drop for those cases is nearly 30p

*November 2025 - Updated Recruitment Privacy Notice*

This Recruitment Privacy Notice (hereinafter “Privacy Notice”) explains how Bolt Technology OÜ and its group companies (hereinafter “Bolt” or “We”) processes your (hereinafter “You” or Data Subject”) personal data during the application and recruitment process.
# *Personal data we process*
We only process the following personal data we need for the activities related to the application and recruitment process:
* *_Contact details_*: such as name and surname, phone number, email address. Sources of collection of data: we get this data from you when applying for a position in Bolt. We may also get this data from a third party who refers you for a position.
* *_Information included in your CV and/or cover letter_*: such as employment history, academic background, skills and experience, languages spoken and written, recommendations and referees and any other information submitted by you. Sources of collection of data: we get this data from you when applying for a position in Bolt. We may also get this data from the referees that you provide.
* *_Information related to assessing your suitability_*: such as information given in screening questionnaires, personality assessment questionnaires, interviews, and test results undertaken during the recruitment process. Sources of collection of data: we get this data from you when applying for a position in Bolt. Some data is generated during the recruitment process. We may also receive this data from third-party tools we use for recruitment-related assessments.
* *_Copy of identification document_*: such as ID or passport copy. Sources of collection of data: we get this data from you prior to entering into the employment contract.
* *_Compensation and payment or benefits related information_*: such as salary, bank account details. Sources of collection of data: we get this data from you prior to entering into the contract. Some data is generated during the process of preparing the agreement.
* *_Employment visa sponsorship related information_*: such as information about whether you need sponsorship for employment visa status and related identity, travel and working documents.
* *_Criminal record checks if required by the law_*: Source of collection of data: we get this data from you when applying for a position which requires such background checks.
* *_General communications_*: such as recruitment process related e-mails or other communications. Sources of collection of data: this data is generated during the recruitment process.
* *_Audio or video recordings of interviews_*: We may also get the data from external recruiters and agencies who carry out the recruitment process on behalf of Bolt as a partner. In our application form you can find questions which are intended to help us learn about the candidates applying to Bolt. # *Recipients*
* In some circumstances we are legally obliged to share information with external recipients. We can also respond to requests, such as those from law enforcement agencies, when we have a good-faith belief that the response is required by law in that jurisdiction or furthers a public interest task, affects users in that jurisdiction, and is consistent with internationally recognised standards. In any scenario, we’ll always satisfy ourselves that we have a lawful basis on which to share the information, and we’ll make sure that we document our decision.

These include providers of recruitment software, applicant tracking systems, assessment and testing tools, video interviewing platforms, and scheduling or communication tools. Such third parties process personal data only on our documented instructions and in accordance with applicable data protection laws. We require all such providers to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect the confidentiality and security of personal data and to use it solely for the purposes of providing their services to us in connection with recruitment.
* We generally do not transfer your personal data outside of the European Union (EU) or the European Economic Area (EEA), nor to such third country or international organization, where the level of data protection of which the European Commission has not considered adequate. You have the right to obtain additional information about the transfer of your personal data by sending the relevant request at [privacy@bolt.eu|mailto:privacy@bolt.eu].
# *Your rights*
_Your right of access_
* you have the right to know, whether personal data concerning you are being processed or not, what is the purpose of processing and what are the categories of personal data. Besides, to whom the personal data is disclosed (especially the recipients in third countries), for how long the personal data is retained and what are your rights concerning rectification, erasure and restriction of the processing.
_Your right to rectification_
* you have the right to demand rectification of the personal data concerning you if the data are inaccurate or incomplete.
_Your right to erasure_
* in some cases, you have the right to demand erasure of the personal data concerning you, for example in case when you withdraw your consent and there are no other legal grounds for the processing of the personal data.
_Your right to restriction of processing_
* You have the right to ask us to restrict the processing of your information in certain circumstances. This means that your data can only be used for certain things, such as legal claims or to exercise legal rights.
_Your right to object to processing_
* you have the right to object the processing of personal data, which is processed based on the legitimate interest, including profiling. Upon objection, we will no longer process the personal data unless we demonstrate compelling legitimate grounds for the processing which override your interests, rights and freedoms.
_Your right to data portability_
* if processing of your personal data is based on your consent or the contract with us and the data processing is carried out by automated means, then you have the right to receive the personal data concerning you, which you have provided to us, in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format. Also, you have the right to claim to transmit those personal data to another data controller if it is technically possible.
_Your right to request an explanation_
* in certain circumstances, you may have the right to receive a clear and meaningful explanation of how an AI system was involved in a decision about you, and the key factors that led to that decision.
# *Retention of personal data*
Your personal data shall not be kept for longer than is necessary for the recruitment process as following:
* If you are not selected for the position, then we will store your data for 3 years to resolve possible disputes arising from the recruitment process.
* If we conclude an employment contract with you, then we will store the personal data collected during the recruitment process for at least the duration of the employment relationship.
# *Dispute resolution*
Disputes relating to the processing of personal data are resolved through customer support ([info@bolt.eu|mailto:info@bolt.eu]) in the first instance. You have the right to contact Bolt's Data Protection Officer ([privacy@bolt.eu|mailto:privacy@bolt.eu]).
Our supervisory authority is the Estonian Data Protection Inspectorate ([www.aki.ee|http://www.aki.ee/]).
# *Making this notice great*
We hope you have found this privacy notice easy to understand. Data protection laws are important. They strengthen rules and enhance your information rights. Many of these rules may appear complicated, but most are grounded in common sense. We take our responsibilities with your data seriously. Bolt will continue to make changes to this privacy notice as part of our commitment to protecting your privacy and affording you even more transparency.

Hi [~accountid:712020:cbcc3a7a-20b1-4e86-9a89-fb6698821d95] - thank you for raising this.

From a data protection perspective, the key point is that Bolt acted on information received from a third party (Q Rental Group OÜ). This means the relevant processing is internal decision-making based on third-party data. While Bolt has a lawful basis for this (legitimate interest and contract performance), the main privacy risk lies in the accuracy and reliability of the information provided by the fleet.

If the details about the alleged “illegal activity” or “debt” are incorrect, the restriction could amount to unfair or unlawful processing under the GDPR.

The core data protection issue is therefore our reliance on third-party information to make an account-level decision about a driver, and the need to ensure that such information is lawfully obtained, accurate, and proportionately used.

Please check with Local Ops to confirm whether the facts shared by the fleet accurately reflect the situation and that we can confidently rely on this data before maintaining or enforcing the restriction.

[~accountid:62615f256cb53d006a6a3fe1] I’ve reviewed the facility agreement at a high level. In my view, *this arrangement is a loan agreement, not akin to a co-financing agreement.* 

In a co-financing arrangement, I understand that funds are provided as an incentive for the fleet to perform on the Bolt platform, subject to achieving specific performance indicators within an agreed period. That is not the case here.

In contrast, this agreement has the key characteristics of a loan, including:

* An obligation to repay the amount advanced (incl. repayable on demand by the lender);
* Interest bearing;
* Fixed term maturity
* Prepayable by the borrower
* Not freely transferrable

On this basis, my view is that, as a general rule, payments under this facility should not be included within the DAC7.

I note, however, that the this agreement is / was subject to tax and TP analysis by Bolt. I wonder if a similar conclusion - i.e. it’s a loan and not something else, e.g. equity, incentive, etc - by tax / TP?

In that case, we believe it remains primarily a_ *_business decision_*_._

*ad 2) Individual lawsuit*

* This is a systematic risk the entire industry faces and will increase following the PWD implementation. We cannot do anything to prevent SKA (or their members) from filing such lawsuits.

*ad 3) Criminal proceedings against Uber*

* In my view, the likelihood of successful criminal proceedings is low to moderate. This complaint seems to be more a PR move rather than an effective legal remedy.
** There are evidentiary gaps – there are not many details, no specific individuals, documents, or concrete incidents identified.
** Criminal offenses referred to in the compliant require certain circumstances to be demonstrated, i.e.
*** Article 286 CC – fraud - intent to deceive;
*** Article 165 CC - real, demonstrable danger to “many persons”;
*** Article 271 CC - false certification - can be committed if official documents are signed (and marketing statements would not qualify as such).
* Most probable outcome of the proceedings: short preliminary inquiry followed by discontinuance or refusal to initiate proceedings. Even if the proceedings are not discontinued, it will take months or even years before all the evidence are gathered and the case if referred to the court.
* However, even if unsuccessful, the criminal proceedings and SKA’s narrative can result in increased media attention and possibly also increased scrutiny and/or negative sentiment towards the industry from the authorities, including GITD and UOKiK.

* continue monitoring SKA’s activity in the social media;

Thanks [~accountid:712020:b2a2738f-c1f1-447c-9b72-29851b5fed3e] - I think it would be useful to have a quick sync on this, as I am not sure contractual necessity (“*CN*”) is the best fit in this context (particularly for Romania).

Although I appreciate that we _could_ rely on CN provided that the ‘Image Rights Authorisation’ form (the “*Form*”) is a valid contract, this approach raises the following issues:

* *‘Common sense’ tes*t: The Form is an optional document (regardless of attendance at the event) that the data subject alone signs, which involves paying no consideration and results in no obvious benefits for the data subject (only for Bolt). This to me sounds more like a consent form rather than an agreement - if we were ever challenged on this, a court or regulator may take the same view. I appreciate there are some IP considerations here as well, but from a very high level POV I still think this is worth flagging.
* *Other regulatory guidance*: Guidance from privacy regulators in other countries on this topic seem to suggest that consent is the expected legal basis for taking and using photos at events (see the Irish DPC’s guidance [here|https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/faqs/topical-data-protection-issues/when-i-am-attending-public-event-can-organisers-take-promotional-photographs-me-without-my-consent]). Obviously this is not directly applicable from a legal POV, but the logic still applies.
* *Utility re the RO Civil Code*: Article 73 of the Romanian Civil Code allows individuals to “_prohibit or prevent the reproduction, in any way_” of their image. The existence of a contract does not act as an exception to this, meaning that even if the participants sign the Form, if they subsequently objected to the use of their image in marketing, we would still have to honour this request and stop ongoing use of their image. The only reason that having a contract would benefit us here would be to entitle Bolt to damages for early termination - this does not appear to be the case based on the limited terms in the Form. As such, what is the benefit of trying to rely on contractual necessity when in practice the participant can still object? Surely this just creates scope for more confusion?

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
{color:#4c9aff}*In terms of how I think this affects our approach:*{color}

* [~accountid:712020:548c71a6-d1f4-404d-9c5e-482bc0de371a] - Are you confident that, under RO requirements, this [form|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1mS6vDHNpypHwrsGVrInnYVOjSKj5q8J2Su769Ab7GBQ/edit?tab=t.0] would count as a valid contract? If so, is there a reason why the document does not contain any withdrawal mechanisms / protections for Bolt should the individual wish to terminate the arrangement (just for my own awareness)?
* Although we *_could_* leave the document as-is and rely on contractual necessity (rather than consent) as the legal basis, I query whether this make practical sense because: (i) we would still effectively need to action objection requests (per requirements under Romanian law); and (ii) reliance on this legal basis seems confusing in the circumstances. My preference would therefore be to do the following:
** (1) Change the ‘withdrawal language’ to “_I am aware that I may request to revoke my authorisation to the use of my image at any time by reaching out to [EMAIL], which will be considered in accordance with applicable requirements_” - This covers us against allegations that we are ignoring requirements under the RO Civil Code, while also keeping the language neutral in case we want to try to maintain that we are relying on CN rather than consent.
** (2) Add consent as a legal basis to the privacy notice, as well as the phrase “_as applicable_” - I think omitting this legal basis is odd. I think we can add it to the privacy notice but use this qualifying language to keep the door open for arguing in favour of both consent and CN as needed.
** (3) Maintain the approach that if a Romanian participant objects, we must honour that request and stop using their image in marketing materials.
*** Just to make sure we have properly kicked the tyres on this, [~accountid:712020:b2a2738f-c1f1-447c-9b72-29851b5fed3e] do you disagree?
* In any case, this is not a huge deal for the current ticket - the event is small and as long as we have objection mechanisms in place, the contents of the form would be defendable either way.

Hi [~accountid:635ba1b276b91b62562e3686] before you commit accepting the risks, please read all the risks involved:

*1. Overall assessment*

The NDA is heavily one-sided in Airbus’s favour, designed for large corporate suppliers.
For an RFI or pre-contractual stage, the overall risk level is low to moderate, but there are several clauses that expose Bolt to legal or operational burdens that should be understood before signing.

None of the risks are immediately disqualifying for participation, but Bolt would carry unlimited liability for certain breaches, even minor ones, and limited flexibility in how it shares Airbus’s information internally.

*2. Major Risks for Bolt*

h3. *1. One-sided disclosure rights (Article 3 – “Other Disclosures”)*

*Issue:*
Airbus may freely share Bolt’s confidential information across all its group companies and subcontractors worldwide.
In contrast, Bolt may share Airbus’s information *only with subcontractors approved in writing by Airbus*.

*Risk:*

* Operational delays: Bolt would need written consent to involve group entities or vendors (e.g., analytics, RFI support, or cloud partners).
* Breach risk: If Bolt shares Airbus information with any unapproved internal affiliate (e.g., Bolt Operations OÜ) — even for legitimate business purposes — that could technically be a *breach of the NDA*.

*Business impact:* Low in practice if Bolt limits access internally, but it creates *administrative and compliance friction*.

*2. Unlimited indemnity and liability (Article 6.3 – Indemnity)*

*Issue:*
Bolt must *indemnify Airbus against “all damages, losses, claims, liabilities, costs and expenses”* arising from any breach — with *no cap on liability*.

*Risk:*

* Even a minor accidental disclosure or system breach could expose Bolt to *unlimited claims*, including Airbus’s internal costs and third-party damages.
* Airbus’s group-wide sharing of data increases the exposure because any Airbus entity could claim loss.

*Business impact:* This is the *most material legal risk*. 

*3. No recognition of the Bolt Group (Article 3 and definitions)*

*Issue:*
The NDA is signed by *Bolt Services UK Ltd*, but it doesn’t permit sharing with *Bolt Operations OÜ* or other Bolt affiliates.

*Risk:*

* Bolt’s legal and operational teams in Tallinn or other jurisdictions cannot legally access Airbus’s materials.
* To stay compliant, all RFI-related work must be handled *solely within the entity that signs (Bolt Services UK Ltd)*.

*Business impact:*
Medium — creates operational inefficiency and data-siloing for internal collaboration.

*4. Arbitration in Paris under ICC rules (Article 10 – Dispute Management)*

*Issue:*
Disputes are resolved under *ICC arbitration seated in Paris*, with *English law governing*.

*Risk:*

* Very *costly dispute process* if anything goes wrong — arbitration fees typically exceed €100k.
* Procedural mismatch (English law but French seat) can create jurisdictional complexity.
* Practically, Bolt would not pursue or defend arbitration for an RFI-stage NDA.

*Business impact:* Low if no dispute arises, but *very high-cost exposure* if triggered.

*5. Overreaching export control and sanctions compliance (Article 7.2)*

*Issue:*
Bolt must ensure compliance not only with EU/UK laws but also *US, French, German, Spanish, and Canadian* export/sanctions regimes.

*Risk:*

* The clause is disproportionate for a simple information exchange.
* Bolt could theoretically be in breach if a third-party tool (e.g., US-based cloud service) is deemed non-compliant under a foreign sanctions list.

*Business impact:* U*nrealistic compliance scope* for a mobility platform.

*6. Duration and retention of confidentiality obligations (Article 8)*

*Issue:*

* NDA term: 3 years
* Confidentiality survives for 5 years after termination

*Risk:*

* Obligations last up to *8 years*, which is longer than industry norm (2–3 years).
* Extended data retention obligations create *burden on record management*.

*Business impact:* Increases internal compliance effort.

* *How will the human review look like and how do we define “human in the loop” in this context?*
** Added a flow chart below to describe the auto-decline flow and indicate where there is a human in the loop ([figma link|https://www.figma.com/board/ph1inLjWYWGT03U8MdH0Yp/Document-auto-decline-flow?node-id=0-1&t=xOzRHAheUKiQbA1v-1]).
!Screenshot 2025-11-19 at 15.29.26.png|width=996,alt="Screenshot 2025-11-19 at 15.29.26.png"!
* *What is the expected impact on the driver when a document is auto-declined, are they blocked from driving, delayed, or something else?*
** 1st roll-out scope includes *driver registration documents only*
*** Driver lead will receive comms that their document has been declined + the decline reason for the document. They are provided the option to resubmit the document. Comms used by automation are exactly the same ones used in manual processing.
*** Automation will decline a document only once in a row and in case it fails >1  times it leaves it in uploaded status for manual processing in OPS teams work queue.
** 2nd roll-out (in Q1 2026) will also include renewal documents
*** When existing driver/fleet uploads a renewal document the document can get automatically declined providing user the feedback with a reason and asks for resubmission (same comms used as in manual processing)
*** Automation will decline a document only once in a row and in case it fails >1  times it leaves it in uploaded status for manual processing in OPS teams work queue.
* *What feedback is shown to the driver after an auto-decline? Is it specific (e.g. "document was blurry") or generic?*
** Automation uses the same document decline reasons used by ops in manual processing. The decline reasons with messaging are listed [*here*|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1EISu6tR87o781Jm2NzEtdZHPDZMGU4ugyvX9Kp7yKL8/edit?gid=294279118#gid=294279118]*.*
** There is a mapping done between automation failure reasons and the relevant decline reason. Automation always uses the mapped decline reason when decline reasons are rolled out for the market and used in manual processing.
*** 1st roll-out scope has decline reasons in use for all the included documents and failure types.
* *What logic determines the X declines before human review? Is it adaptive (e.g. varies by document type)?*
** Automation declines only *once* before leaving the document processing  to OPS manual processing queue.
* *Is there any ongoing QA on Veritas or Beehive outputs that drive declines?*
** Yes - Veritas has a regular QA process in place for their human reviewers
** For Beehive conflict resolution task there is not. Because → when a task reaches conflict resolution there already is a previous extraction, so Beehive task in this case is the additional confirmation layer enabling error correction.
* *Is appeal data (e.g. successful reversals) used to improve the system?*
** Auto-decline is rolled out only for document types + failure reason combinations which have accuracy higher than 95%. This accuracy will be re-evaluated based on auditing data to continuously validate the decline decision confidence to decide if auto-decline can remain enabled.

Hi [~accountid:712020:85a31a38-edb2-4253-b037-fa5bcad14728] ,

Thanks for all your responses and clarifications.

From a legal standpoint, our view is that the proposed campaign imposes +a certain level of risk+, since focusing the campaign only on couriers who have not worked the last 3 Saturdays, and conditioning the bonus on completing 6+ deliveries, might be seen as introducing a system that nudges scheduling and performance, which could be used as evidence that Bolt organizes, directs, or incentivizes work patterns (one of the key triggers under the employment classification framework).

However, since Malta is currently not among the riskiest jurisdictions when it comes to reclassification, and since the proposed campaign is not materially different from campaigns aimed at reactivating longer-term inactive users (which are already common), we believe this is primarily a business decision.

Our guidance in order to mitigate the risks as much as possible is the following:

# *The campaign should be framed strictly as an output-based incentive* — i.e. _“Complete 6+ deliveries between 17:00–19:00”_ with +no references to required online hours or minimum availability+;
# *The reason for targeting couriers is not disclosed* — meaning we +do not tell couriers (explicitly or implicitly)+ that they are receiving the offer because they didn’t work the last 3 Saturdays;
# +*The campaign remains one-off or short-term*+ — to avoid building a pattern that could indicate systematic control over scheduling.

We believe that, with this structure, the risk is kept within the same category as other output-based incentives, which are considered safer than those tied to online time or acceptance rate. 

Let us know if you’d like us to review the final courier-facing copy before launch, just to make sure the language stays fully aligned.

Thank you!

Thank you for escalating! 
The customer has a negative balance due to a technical issue from Bolt’s end. 

This bug happens with Alternative Payment methods (APMs). APMs don’t have dual messaging — Authorization + Capture. They just have the capture. 
If the payment amount is lower than the captured amount then Bolt will automatically refund the difference. 

In this case the capture was for  20.46 PLN, but order price was just 9.50 PLN. 
This triggered an automatic refund for 10.96 PLN. 

Now when the full refund for 9.5 PLN was issued then it triggered the bug/discrepancy between how the refund was recorded on the payment vs order. The full refund for payment was 20.46 PLN. However, for the order the full refund is 9.5 PLN. 

20.46 PLN - 9.5 PLN = 10.96 PLN. 

How to solve the issue for the customer? 
The customers balance cannot be amended. The only way we can solve the issue for the customer is to issue a Bolt Balance refund. 
Unfortunately, the customer payments team doesn’t have any accesses to issue refunds to to BB. 

Could you please issue a Bolt Balance refund for the customer for 10.96 PLN? You might not be able to issue the refund from the original order as the “refund has already been issued”. Could you please try to issue the refund from customers other recent orders? If you have any issues you might want to check with your team lead as they have higher permissions to refund from old orders.

To ensure that the review is aligned with the intended operational model, we kindly ask you to first provide a *business case* outlining how the team envisions implementing the service.

For example, it would be helpful to clarify:

* Will this be an on-demand or scheduled service, or a combination of both?
* Will the waste be collected from private individuals, commercial businesses (e.g. Airbnbs), or both?
* Do you already have or expect to have sufficient operator supply, and are these fleets licensed or willing to be licensed as waste carriers with ERA?
* What type(s) of waste will be collected (e.g. general household, recyclable, glass, bulky waste)?
* Will the service operate nationwide, or only in select localities (and if so, which ones)?
* Where will the collected waste be delivered — to bring-in sites, licensed waste facilities, or another designated endpoint?

This information will help us scope the applicable licensing, operational, and municipal constraints, and determine the potential platform exposure (if any) under the current legal framework.

As our legal budget is limited — especially at this time of the year — it would be very helpful if the proposal could be as detailed and precise as possible. This will allow external counsel to target their review efficiently and avoid a prolonged back-and-forth of preliminary questions and clarifications.

Looking forward to your input so we can proceed accordingly with exploring the actual feasibility of this exciting idea.

Thanks!

h3. 1. *TL;DR*

_🟢 Low risk_

* *What:* This is a one-time, manual email verification test using a reputable EU vendor.
* *Why it matters:* Email addresses are personal data — if mishandled, this could erode user trust or lead to unintended exposure.
* *Mitigations:* The DPA from MillionVerifier meets expected standards for one-time processing. No sensitive or special category data is involved. Data deletion practices and security controls are documented.

h3. 2. *Summary of feature*

* Bolt plans to manually upload a CSV of email addresses to MillionVerifier’s platform to test their “valid / invalid / risky” classification service.
* The goal is to clean email lists and improve campaign performance.
* The vendor processes data within the EU and claims automated deletion within a year.
* No system integration; this is a one-time test.

h3. 3. *Key privacy observations*

* ✅ *Data minimization*: The only required input is email addresses, no additional personal data.
* ✅ *No profiling or automated decision-making*: Service classifies emails by technical quality, not personal characteristics.
* ✅ *Data retention/deletion*: Data is stored for up to 1 year unless manually deleted earlier. Backups retain files for 5 more days after deletion.
* ✅ *Security controls*: Encrypted transmission, automated processing, regular penetration testing, NDA-bound staff.
* ⚠️ *Broad sub-processor clause*: Consent to new sub-processors is assumed via passive acceptance (i.e., continued use after an update to their Terms or Privacy Policy).
* 🟢 *Support for data subject rights*: Vendor commits to assisting with DSARs, breach notices within 48 hours, and audit support.

Subject line: Data protection & dashcams: What you need to know
Header: Important recommendations for using cameras in your vehicles.
Hero text:
We want to ensure that the Bolt platform continues to uphold the highest data protection standards for our mutual customers. We have recently received enquiries regarding the use of dashcams and cameras in vehicles.
Body:
As a fleet partner, you are considered an independent controller under data protection regulations and are therefore responsible for ensuring that the use of cameras in your fleet complies with local laws and EU regulations.
GREEN BLOCK
Our recommendations for you:
Transparency in vehicles: If cameras are used in your fleet, we strongly recommend that you display warning notices in the affected vehicles that are clearly visible to your passengers. These should include the purpose of the recording, the name of your company as the controller, the storage period and access to further information.
Check documentation: Ensure that your privacy policy clearly covers the processing of video recordings by your vehicles.
Inform drivers: Ensure that your drivers are aware of the correct use of the cameras and their obligation to inform passengers.

WHITE BLOCK
Please note that failure to comply with these requirements may result in legal consequences due to violations of data protection laws.
DARK GREEN BLOCK
While we make these recommendations, we would like to emphasise that, as an independent controller, you decide for yourself whether to follow our advice. However, it is important to note that you may be liable for any violations.
WHITE BLOCK
Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Best regards
Bolt Team

Due to a now fixed bug in the configuration flattening algorithm, we ended up with a node in the database that was missing a specific attribute `fleet_document_type` in the flat representation, but had a `hash` as if it had it to `th_publiclicense`

So when this field was set to `th_publiclicense` in the frontend, the frontend correctly detected the local configuration change and suggested to Save the changes.

The backend in turn checks whether the config was truly changed by flattening the incoming tree and the comparing the new flat representation with the old flat representation by `hash`. And since the hash was the same between the incoming and the existing version of the node, no change would be detected.

Setting the attribute to an empty string and then back to `th_publiclicense` fixed the problem for the most recent config version. The old version is still going to have this behaviour, but it will not affect our lives in the future.

So, there's nothing really to fix.

+*BACKGROUND*+

* As part of Bolt Rewards, Bolt is in a partnership with Olerex (Estonian fuel retailer), and has been since the summer.
** Olerex offers drivers tiered fuel discounts and additional benefits.
* To redeem the offer, Bolt drivers need to do the following:
** 1. Click a hyperlink to access [this page|https://liitu.olerex.ee/bolt], and then enter a unique referral code.
** 2. Register for, or log into, their Olerex account.
** 3. Activate the Bolt discount card on the Olerex platform.
* The arrangement is governed by an existing agreement (English translation is below).
** Between EE entities. 
** Bolt markets Olerex’s discounts to bolt drivers. Once per month, Bolt must inform Olerex about active Bolt Rewards users.
** Olerex must share monthly liquid fuel volumes with Bolt (each based on individual Bolt Rewards Codes).
** No obvious data sharing provisions - Why? (?) 
* Data sharing under the agreement appears to be mutual.
** *Bolt → Olerex*: List of drivers (including referral codes and tier breakdowns), so that Olerex can assign the corresponding tiered discounts to the correct referral code on their side.
*** “_We also have access to Olerex’s self-service environment to make ongoing updates_” - unclear what this means in practice (?) 
** *Olerex → Bolt*: Discount card numbers and corresponding purchase data.
*** NB. Numbers here are different from the referral code, and so we cannot identify the drivers that have used referral codes. As such, Ops wants to add referral codes to the list of data shared.
*** What specifically do we mean by purchase data? It would be helpful to see an example of the redemption data sheet (?) 
* Bolt wants to know which drivers have not used the offer, so that they can contact them and understand why.
* *Request*: Is this data exchange possible, and if so, under what conditions?

+*ANALYSIS*+

* General:
** This kind of data exchange is covered in our privacy notice, and is fine.
* Data Sharing:
** In the first instance, my preference would be to try to enter a full DSA with Olerex. I have prepared this here: [LINK|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1HiK_JgXEOCACXJRuRdgvuJiBEIVjp6o9Hn6DJCYWu54/edit?tab=t.0].
** However, if Olerex pushes back, we can consider light touch / mutual data sharing provisions as a fallback option, as the data sharing here is very low risk.
* Marketing:
** If Bolt is marketing Olerex discounts to Bolt users, we can only do so via _direct_ means with appropriate consents in place.
** If Olerex is marketing Bolt services to Olerex users (unlikely), then we may want to some direct marketing contractual controls (see the DSA).

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Questions:
** Is there currently a DSA in place? If not, why not? Did anyone from Privacy review the original arrangement?
** Could I see an example of the full redemption sheet? What purchase data is being shared?
** What does having access to Olerex’s self-service environment mean in practice? Will we be exchanging any additional data to what ahs been described already?
* Advice:
** Olerex adding redemption codes to the pool of data that they are sharing with us is fine. To be clear - personal data exchange is already happening here.
** Propose the DSA. If Olerex pushes back, we can consider lighter-touch provisions. If Olerex outright refuses, business can proceed at risk (no huge liability risk for us here).
** Provide usual advice re direct marketing. Even though this has gone on for a while, we still need to ensure business has the advice.

👋 Hey there!
If you need a *report*, please refer to FleetX (DriverX). If your request concerns an *invoice*, follow these steps:

1. Open the **Client page in Admin**: [link|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-rides/clients?tz=Europe%2FTallinn&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D].
2. Enter the Fleet or Driver ID in the **External ID** filter field.
3. Open the driver or fleet profile.
4. Go to the **Invoice tasks** tab.
   * If you see *Invoice sum too small*, no commission invoice was generated because the driver either owed no commission or had more compensation than commission.
   * If you encounter any other error, please let us know.
5. Commission invoices for the entire history of the fleet/driver are available either under **Invoice tasks** or **Partner Invoices**.

Best regards,

Hi all, 

Sharing answer from the local team about Courier bag processes and Tablets for Merchants:

*Bags:*

We send SMS invitations to couriers to visit our office and pick up their delivery bag. If a courier already has a Wolt or Glovo thermal bag, they can simply send us a photo of the bag together with their ID, and we activate them without requiring an office visit. If they don’t have a thermal bag, they need to come to the office to purchase one of ours. We give them the bag upfront and charge them one week later.We’re also running a campaign: the standard bag price is *100 GEL*, but the actual price is reduced based on how many orders the courier completes in their first week.
 For example:

* Deliver 20 orders → price becomes *80 GEL* (100 - 20)
* Deliver 100 orders in the first 7 days → the bag becomes *free*

Also, if the courier has less then 5 orders delivered, we return bag and adjust the amount we adjusted before. So if he has -100 GEL bag adjustment, we adjust +100 GEL. If he has more then 5 orders delivered we don't return the bag.

*Tablets:*

For Sunmi V2s and Sunmi L2s we buy from HQ
We also source Samsung tablets locally

Please let me know if you have any additional questions.

Best regards,
Roberts

{quote}Dear [*Name*],


Thank you for bringing this matter to our attention. We fully understand your concern regarding the video shared online and the driver’s behaviour during the trip.


Please note that drivers using the Bolt platform are independent providers and not Bolt employees. If a driver records or shares a video, they act as an independent data controller under data protection law and are solely responsible for ensuring that such processing complies with the GDPR and local legislation, including obtaining any required consent. Bolt does not provide, install or control any recording devices, and we do not have access to or the ability to remove or delete such content.


That said, we take reports of this nature very seriously. We have escalated the matter internally and contacted the driver’s fleet owner to inform them of the situation and request that the video be removed as soon as possible. We have also reminded them of their obligations under data protection law and the standards expected from drivers using the Bolt platform.


You may also wish to report this incident to the authorities, who can investigate the matter further. Should they need trip or driver details, they can contact us at [*add* *local email]*, and the responsible team will provide the necessary information to support their investigation. Bolt will fully cooperate with any requests received from the competent authorities. In addition, we recommend also reporting the video to the platform it was posted on.


We sincerely regret the distress this incident has caused and thank you for taking the time to alert us. Please don’t hesitate to reach out to our customer support team if you have any further questions or concerns.


Sincerely,{quote}

➡️ Since drivers are independent controllers, Bolt cannot force them to remove the video. That being said, I checked the YouTube link shared by the rider and the video is showing as unavailable on my end, which suggests that it was taken down.

{quote}Dear [*FO Name*],


We are reaching out regarding a serious privacy concern reported to Bolt involving one of your drivers, [*Driver’s full name*], in connection with a ride that took place on [*ride date]*.


 According to the report, the driver allegedly recorded a passenger without consent and subsequently shared the video on social media. The content in question has caused significant distress to the passenger, and this type of conduct is wholly inconsistent with the standards expected of drivers using the Bolt platform.


We take such matters extremely seriously. We urge you to immediately review this incident and take appropriate action in line with your responsibilities as a data controller. In particular, we strongly recommend that the video be removed from all social media platforms without delay, given that it appears to have been recorded and shared without the passenger’s consent. Please also remind the driver involved of their obligations to treat all passengers respectfully and to comply with applicable data protection laws.


As a reminder, you are considered an independent data controller under applicable data protection regulations. This means that you are responsible for ensuring that any recording or sharing of passenger data complies with the GDPR and local legislation, particularly regarding transparency, consent, and lawful processing.


If any of your drivers use cameras or other recording devices aboard their vehicle, please ensure that:

* passengers are clearly informed through visible notices that a recording is taking place;
* the purpose, controller details, data retention period, and a reference to a privacy notice are made available; and
* any processing of recordings is conducted lawfully and securely.

We also recommend that you review your internal privacy policies and ensure that they clearly describe how personal data from recordings is processed and protected. Sharing any customer-related content publicly, especially without consent, constitutes a serious violation of privacy rights and may have legal consequences.


While we provide this guidance, we would like to reiterate that as independent data controllers, you have the autonomy to decide how to act on this advice. However, you remain accountable for ensuring compliance with data protection law and for any breaches arising from your or your drivers’ actions.


Please confirm once you have reviewed the situation and taken the necessary steps in response to this report.
If you have any questions or require further clarification, please don’t hesitate to contact us.


Kind regards,{quote}

Hi [~accountid:641aac4f9d6383e32a32c047], I have forwarded you the full reply from external counsel (DLA) regarding Whistleblowing in Sweden in your email.

*Summary:*

Under Swedish law, companies with *50–250 employees* can share certain reporting and investigation procedures with others of similar size but *cannot share contact or follow-up* with the reporting person. This means that for reports made within Sweden, *all direct communication with the whistleblower must remain within Bolt Sweden*, even if the investigation is coordinated or supported by the global Ethics Committee.

DLA noted that the Swedish Whistleblowing Act protects only specific categories of reports – namely, breaches of EU or Swedish law (e.g. public procurement, financial services, product safety, public health, environmental or data protection breaches) and certain serious work-related irregularities of public interest. They recommend updating the policy to:

* clearly distinguish which topics are legally protected under Swedish law;
* include *details for both internal and external reporting channels*, including contact details for designated Swedish authorities;
* expand the list of *protected individuals* (to include interns, prospective and former employees, volunteers, shareholders, and board members); and
* consider discouraging *anonymous reports* as they complicate investigations.

Hi [~accountid:712020:f50af85a-3d8b-4b5c-b19d-ad552b86d158] ,

Given the *low value (~EUR 4,000 annually for 11 employees)* and low-risk nature of this contract, *there are no major risks.* However, there are still a few clauses from ClassPass Corporate Program Terms and Conditions worth highlighting where redlines or clarifications could enhance Bolt’s position or reduce ambiguity.

----

h3. 1. *Unilateral Amendment Right*

*Clause*: ClassPass T&Cs, Section 1.3 and 2.2

{quote}ClassPass may change the agreement terms or features of the program unilaterally, with changes effective upon posting.{quote}

*Risk*: This exposes Bolt to *unforeseen commercial or legal terms*, especially during renewal.

*Redline Suggestion*:

{quote}“Any material changes to this Agreement shall require the *prior written consent of the Partner*. Continued use of the Program shall not constitute deemed acceptance of such changes.”{quote}

----

h3. 2. *Termination Rights – ClassPass Can Terminate at Will*

*Clause*: Section 6.2

{quote}“ClassPass may terminate this Agreement at any time for any reason upon 30 days’ notice.”{quote}

*Risk*: One-sided right that Bolt does not enjoy. Ideally, *termination rights should be mutual*.

*Redline Suggestion*:

{quote}“Either Party may terminate this Agreement for convenience by giving 30 days’ prior written notice.”{quote}

----

h3. 3. *Auto-Renewal + Early Termination Fee*

*Clauses*:

* Section 6.1: Auto-renewal
* Section 4.3: Payment non-cancellable
* Order Form: “Fees are non-refundable”

*Risk*: Auto-renewal paired with non-cancellable obligations *locks Bolt into an unwanted renewal*, even if Bolt notifies termination late.

*Redline Suggestion*:

{quote}Add a clause to allow *early termination without future payment obligations for the whole Term.*{quote}

----

h3. 4. *Limitation of Liability – Extremely Low Cap*

*Clause*: Section 9

{quote}ClassPass's total liability capped at *USD 100 or total fees paid*, whichever is higher.{quote}

*Risk*: This cap is *disproportionately low*, even for low-value contracts, and offers *no real recourse for Bolt* in case of data breaches, IP infringement, etc.

*Bolt Playbook* recommends:

* A supplier’s liability cap of *100% of fees paid/payable*, or a reasonable fixed amount.
* Certain categories (confidentiality, data, IP) should have *carve-outs or super caps*.

*Redline Suggestion*:

{quote}“Notwithstanding the foregoing, ClassPass’s liability for breaches of data protection, confidentiality, or intellectual property shall be subject to a separate cap of *USD 20,000*.”{quote}

----

h3. 5. *Governing Law and Jurisdiction – California, USA*

*Clause*: Section 11.2 – California law and San Luis Obispo courts

*Risk*: *Unfavourable jurisdiction* for a Malaysian entity. Litigating in California would be costly and impractical.

*Redline Suggestion*:

{quote}“This Agreement shall be governed by the laws of Malaysia, and the Parties submit to the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Malaysia.”{quote}

----

h3. 6. *Intellectual Property / Branding*

*Clause*: Section 7

{quote}Use for marketing and promotional purposes in connection with ClassPass business.{quote}

*Redline Suggestion*:

{quote}“Any use of the Partner’s trademarks or logos must be subject to *prior written approval*, and may be revoked at any time.”{quote}

* They show that we have a notable number of users with invalid documents (*verified_not_ok*). Most of these cases have the *INVALID_DOCUMENT (230)* reason, which means the documents passed the government database (gov DB) check but were later determined to be invalid. Some cases have the *FAILED_TO_AUTHENTICATE_DOCUMENT (157)* reason, indicating that the documents were not found in the gov DB (and many of these are indeed invalid). I manually reviewed around *20 cases* and did not find any false positives.
* There are also two cases with the DOCUMENT_LOOKS_FAKE (1) reason, but it looks like an agent's mistake.
* During the test, an issue with *Veriff verifications* also surfaced, leading to a considerable number of failed cases. This mainly happens because a Veriff flow run can contain multiple photos (for example, unsuccessful or overexposed attempts). Previously, only one photo was used for OCR and human review, which could sometimes be unreadable. For human review, this issue has now been addressed — all photos are now provided to reviewers. However, we still observe failures with reasons such as *DOCUMENT_DETAILS_NOT_VISIBLE (5)* and *MISSING_DATA (102)*, since agents do not always check all the provided photos.

*Re-run with all photos (84 cases):*

* *62 (~74%)* – verified
* *12 (~14%)* – verified_not_ok
* *10 (~12%)* – failed

*Next Steps / Suggested Actions*
Given the high number of *verified_not_ok* cases, it’s possible that many of them represent valid scenarios — for example, users with lost documents, name changes (e.g., after marriage), and similar [cases.To|http://cases.To] improve the process, we could change the current approach:

# Instead of blocking such documents and asking users to contact Customer Support (CS), we could *automatically revoke the documents* and ask users to *complete the verification flow again* without involving CS. We can likely reduce the number of such cases by *instructing agents* on how to manually verify multiple photos correctly. Later, *OCR should also be adapted* to handle multi-photo verification automatically. We could also consider *re-running the failed reverifications* once these adjustments are in place.

Example: EOS FR shouldn’t charge FR VAT to EOS DE and EOS DE this VAT as expense/cost to us but EOS FR issue directly the invoice Bolt (VAT reverse charged)

VAT deductibility:

Bolt Ops will contract EOS to ensure driver/fleet debt against car lessor is paid. Can we treat such expense as deductible for VAT purposes before the debt obligation is passed to Bolt as debtor? Yes — in most EU countries, the guarantor can deduct VAT if the guarantee relates to its taxable business activity.

Because:

# The debt collection costs are incurred to protect the guarantor’s business assets.
# Hiring a debt collector is a cost directly connected to the guarantor’s economic activity, even if the guarantee payment has not yet been made.
# EU VAT case law (including CJEU) says:
 Input VAT is deductible if the expenditure is made for the purpose of the taxable business, even if no taxable supply results directly.
# The guarantor is the one receiving the service (debt collection), so the invoice is addressed to the guarantor, not the lessee.

VAT deduction is not allowed if the guarantor performs only VAT-exempt activities (e.g., exempt financial services) but it is not our case.

In this scenario, the guarantor (Bolt) is not replacing the debtor, nor paying anything yet. But the guarantor incurs the cost to protect itself from future liability.

EU VAT law allows deduction of input VAT when expenses are incurred:

* to prevent costs,
* to reduce business risk,
* to protect taxable activity,
* even if they do not produce any immediate taxable output.

This is consistent with CJEU reasoning in cases such as:

* C-408/98 Abbey National
* C-465/03 Kretztechnik

What I found about German approach doesn’t differ from EU practice

In Germany, the guarantor can deduct VAT from the debt-collection agency’s invoice even if:

* the lessee (debtor) has not paid,
* the guarantor has _not yet_ fulfilled the guarantee,
* the guarantor hires the debt-collector to recover the debt or prevent the guarantee from being triggered.

IF the guarantee was issued in the course of its taxable business activity. Then input VAT is deductible if the cost is economically linked to the taxable business activity (§ 15 Abs. 1 Nr. 1 UStG).

*Update: this topic has now been resolved.*

When responding to official data requests from authorities, Bolt must share personal data *only in a controlled and documented digital format*, ensuring data minimization, access restrictions, and auditability.

h4. 1. *Approved Format and Storage*

* Data must be prepared and disclosed *in a Google Document*.
* The document must be stored in the *designated shared Google Drive folder* created for law enforcement requests.
* Access to the document must be *restricted to “Only people with access can open the link.”* Public or company-wide links are strictly prohibited.
* The shared Google Doc must contain *only the specific personal data requested* — any unrelated or excessive data must be excluded before disclosure.

h4. 2. *Transmission to Authorities*

* Data should be shared *only after validation of the request’s authenticity, legality, and proportionality* (steps 1–3 in the CS Privacy Compliance procedure).
* Disclosure occurs *electronically*, by sending the prepared Google Doc link or an exported copy via an official and verifiable communication channel with the requesting authority.
* *No personal data can ever be shared over the phone*, even in emergency or life-threatening situations.

h4. 3. *Internal Review and Approval*

* Certain categories of data (e.g., driver order history, financial transactions, or identity documents) require *prior approval from the CS Privacy Compliance Team* before sharing.
* More sensitive data (e.g., offences, background checks, special category data, or employee data) requires *Risk Team approval*.
* After disclosure, the CS Privacy Compliance Team performs a *post-release review* within 5 days to confirm that the data was shared correctly and proportionally.

h4. 4. *Data Minimization and Redaction*

* When creating the disclosure file:
** Include *only the user type* data relevant to the request (driver, rider, courier, etc.).
** *Exclude cross-user data* — e.g., when sharing a driver’s order history, omit passenger details.
** Remove any metadata or content not explicitly requested.
** Confirm that *no excessive data* (e.g., other users’ data or unrelated logs) is included.

h4. 5. *Audit Trail*

* All data disclosures must be traceable:
** Each disclosure is linked to a *Service Desk (SD) ticket*.
** Approvals, redactions, and risk assessments are documented in internal notes.
** Post-release findings and potential oversharing are reported to the *Privacy Legal Service Desk*.



Find more information in the Procedure for handling Law Enforcement Requests: [https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/IMS/pages/5568594627/Law+Enforcement+and+Authority+Requests+Procedure+LER|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/IMS/pages/5568594627/Law+Enforcement+and+Authority+Requests+Procedure+LER|smart-link] .

The specific details of the format used to share data with law enforcement agencies upon request can be found here: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/83887|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/83887]
