On a preliminary approach, I think that all the monetary measures related to the incentive score would trigger VAT implications that are already in place in our current setup. I mean,

* Discounts *must be compulsorily shown separately in invoices* (i.e., in a separate row) so when the proposed measures are meant to come into effect, pls LMK to reach out the commerce (billing) team and make sure that they adapt the invoices to comply with this requirement.
* *Contractual penalties* (such as the penalties related to low driving scores) linked to the usage of the car and aimed at discouraging reckless driving and/or any other type of misbehavior *are subject to VAT*. Therefore, drivers with low scores who are charged with these sort of penalties will have to bear the cost of the penalty plus the cost of VAT.

Hi [~accountid:621c82b8a12450006885df74] reviewed the NDA from SLB and *unfortunately we can’t sign* it in its current form. 

* It’s *one-way*, meaning only Bolt is bound to protect *their* information, not the other way around. That’s not a position we can agree to, even for low-risk deals. 
* As the draft was provided in non-editable PDF format, we’re unable to make direct tracked changes. However, in the interest of time I’ve set out the changes Bolt would require before signing ➡️ nothing aggressive, just standard mutual protections.

Please advise the customer that we kindly request the following amendments to ensure the agreement aligns with standard mutual confidentiality terms and practical compliance norms:

# *Preamble / Clause 1 (Definition + Confidentiality Obligation)*
We kindly request replacing the definition of “Recipient” (currently defined as Bolt only) with a *mutual framework* referencing “Disclosing Party” and “Receiving Party”. This ensures confidentiality obligations apply to *both parties*, and would involve adjusting the operative language to:
“Each party (the ‘Receiving Party’) undertakes to keep the Confidential Information of the other (the ‘Disclosing Party’) confidential…”
This is standard market practice and ensures both parties are equally protected, even if the counterparty expects to disclose more information.
# *Clause 2 (Term)*
We kindly request reducing the confidentiality obligation duration from *seven (7) years* to *three (3) years*, which is more typical for commercial discussions and reduces long-term administrative burden.
# *Clause 3 (Return/Destruction)*
We kindly request a carve-out allowing each party to retain copies of Confidential Information as required by *law, regulation, or internal compliance/archive policies*. This ensures the clause is operationally feasible.
# *Clause 6 (Publicity / References)*
We kindly request a small adjustment to allow for use of the counterparty’s name or logo *with prior written consent, not to be unreasonably withheld*. This would allow for future case studies or customer reference use, subject to approval.
# *Clause 5 (Disclosure by Law)*
We kindly request adding a requirement for the recipient to *give advance written notice* of any legally compelled disclosure, where legally permitted. This allows the discloser to take protective steps if needed.

Hi team, 

Thank you for escalating! 
The customer has a negative balance due to a technical issue from Bolt’s end. 

This bug happens with Alternative Payment methods (APMs). APMs don’t have dual messaging — Authorization + Capture. They just have the capture. 
If the payment amount is lower than the captured amount then Bolt will automatically refund the difference. 

In this case the capture was for 26.40 PLN, but order price was just 17.55 PLN (cancellation fee + customers previous negative balance). 
This triggered an automatic refund for 8.85 PLN. 

Now when the full refund for 10.00 PLN was issued then it triggered the bug/discrepancy between how the refund was recorded on the payment vs order. The full refund for payment was 26.40 PLN. However, for the order the full refund is 10 PLN. 

26.40 PLN - 10 PLN = 16.40 PLN. 

How to solve the issue for the customer? 
The customers balance cannot be amended. The only way we can solve the issue for the customer is to issue a Bolt Balance refund. 
Unfortunately, the customer payments team doesn’t have any accesses to issue refunds to to BB. 

Could you please issue a Bolt Balance refund for the customer for 16.40 PLN? You might not be able to issue the refund from the original order as the “refund has already been issued”. Could you please try to issue the refund from customers other recent orders? If you have any issues you might want to check with your team lead as they have higher permissions to refund from old orders. 

Please note that this has been escalated to payment engineers to fix here.

Thank you for escalating! 
The customer has a negative balance due to a technical issue from Bolt’s end. 

This bug happens with Alternative Payment methods (APMs). APMs don’t have dual messaging — Authorization + Capture. They just have the capture. 
If the payment amount is lower than the captured amount then Bolt will automatically refund the difference. 

In this case the capture was for 69.67 PLN, but order price was just 10.00 PLN (cancellation fee). 
This triggered an automatic refund for 59.67 PLN. 

Now when the full refund for 10.00 PLN was issued then it triggered the bug/discrepancy between how the refund was recorded on the payment vs order. The full refund for payment was 69.67 PLN. However, for the order the full refund is 10.00 PLN. 

69.67 PLN - 10.00 PLN = 59.67 PLN. 

How to solve the issue for the customer? 
The customers balance cannot be amended. The only way we can solve the issue for the customer is to issue a Bolt Balance refund. 
Unfortunately, the customer payments team doesn’t have any accesses to issue refunds to to BB. 

Could you please issue a Bolt Balance refund for the customer for 59.67 PLN? You might not be able to issue the refund from the original order as the “refund has already been issued”. Could you please try to issue the refund from customers other recent orders? If you have any issues you might want to check with your team lead as they have higher permissions to refund from old orders. 

Please note that this has been escalated to payment engineers to fix here.

As part of the ongoing work to expand the value proposition, most of the metrics for all distance buckets are now available from CI. However, there’s one key metric — average_trip_distance, that’s missing and is quite important for calculating both rider net price and driver earnings.
Since we’re using normalized ASP, and the normalization process depends on average_trip_distance, the absence of this metric in CI means that the net price gap and driver earning gap are currently unavailable for all distances.
You might remember that we previously agreed to use the weighted average of GMV for all distances. However, since we don’t have distance-bucket-level data for the cities now being sourced from CI, that approach isn’t feasible. I considered reverting to the original formula (without the weighted average), but even that isn’t possible because average_trip_distance is required for one of the key metrics used in those calculations.

After discussion with vish, we decided to proceed without normalizing

Hey, just to sense check - is payment by standing order acceptable to us and feasible?
This licence is a fixed 12-month term with automatic renewal for successive terms unless we give prior notice; renewals can reprice to “then prevailing market rate,” and terms >12 months see RPI indexation. We must give 3 months’ notice and *cannot exit before the end date* of the current term. This is not the usual flexibility that we have - is this acceptable to you, operationally? I don’t want to cut across any commercial negotiations on this. If this is not acceptable I can suggest alternative drafting e.g. at the very least remove the lock-in period. At the moment we have no right to terminate mid-term, but the licence fee is not major so it may be acceptable to you. 

* Clause 4(a)(iii) states 6% above base rate on all overdue payments - this is on a high side. Market standard is 2-4%. 
* Clause 4(a)(ii) [should be (ix)] states: “you shall notify us of any defects via email within 24 hours throughout occupancy of your unit(s)/office(s).” Since it is unmanned can we please remove this as we are not going to be aware. 
* Clause 4(a)(iii) [should be ( x)] states: “arrange to have your unit(s)/office(s) contents be PAT tested on an annual basis.” This reads like we have to arrange for electrical testing of any of their contents? Either we remove this or we can accept “arrange any portable electrical equipment introduced by you into the unit(s)/office(s) is maintained in a safe condition and, where reasonably required, tested by a competent person.”
* Please note the one-off admin/setup fee we have to pay on first invoice - 299 plus VAT and fees for additional furniture - but it is not clear what furniture is already included in the base fee - worth clarifying this. Clause 4(e). Also note the once a month cleaning fee - will this still be charged even if nobody attends? If this is already included in your fee calculation then that is fine but just wanted to flag. Ideally we would just have an all inclusive monthly licence fee without extras. 
* Clause 10(e) - can we amend it to 14 days

Following internal discussion and review of the Fleet Agreements we have in place, Legal view is the following:

# From a legal perspective, implementing courier-level blocking based on low acceptance rate does raise *reclassification risk* under the Maltese framework — particularly in light of S.L. 452.127. That said, as highlighted in the [Features Matrix|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1ZuRlUQXtVwpZlsGnGIwfN_dYrK4LTRf1Mv55hwgWHrk/edit?gid=1905173752#gid=1905173752] prepared by central legal, this type of action would reduce our model’s legal defendability by around *45%*. While that’s not negligible, it is also true that Malta is currently not among the riskiest jurisdictions when it comes to reclassification (for now), especially if this is applied exclusively to fleet couriers, as you proposed. In that case, we believe it remains primarily a *business decision*.
# However, it’s important to flag that the *existing Fleet Agreements* (at least the ones you provided) do not include any clauses authorizing courier-level performance enforcement (e.g., blocking couriers for low acceptance rate). They only contain fleet-level KPIs, and there are no unilateral amendment clauses.
Therefore, if the team wants to proceed, our preferred approach would be entering into *new agreements* with the fleets. Our recommendation is to adopt the latest [*global Fleet Agreement template*|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1igrgRwUHHPbrUqIA3HfqllnJmYoZmJ-8AQeoyW6MVJM/edit?tab=t.0], in which we can include clear courier-level performance obligations, and it can be amended on Bolt’s unilateral decision, as long we give a 15 days notice.
Ideally, if the team decides to move forward with this, we would share this global template with *Fenech & Fenech* for their review and, subject to their approval, we could start using it for:
a) All *new fleet partnerships*, and
b) A *phased update process* for fleets already operating under the old agreement.
# *That said, if this is critical for the business and you cannot afford to wait*, we can adopt an interim approach by relying on the General Terms & Conditions and the existing communication and blocking process. 
This is possible because, even though the General T&Cs (and the Fleet Agreement) are formally between Bolt and the fleet, blocking individual couriers can still be framed as a limitation on the fleet’s access to the platform — particularly where specific courier behavior affects the fleet’s overall performance. In this context, we can rely on clauses 4.3.2 and 4.3.3 of the General T&Cs, which prohibit:
_”4.3.2. activity that materially interferes with the arrangement of services via the Bolt Food Platform (including offering services without an intention to fulfil them);_
_4.3.3. activity that is materially inconsistent with a genuine intention to provide delivery services to Clients.”_
These provisions give us a fallback legal basis to temporarily block underperforming couriers as part of managing the fleet’s obligations under the General T&Cs.

Main research:

h3. 1. Overview of the request

The letter comes from the *Head of the Lublin Customs and Tax Office (Lubelski Urząd Celno–Skarbowy)*. It requests disclosure of *personal data of two Bolt users* related to rides in *Lublin*:

* *User 1:* Ride on *1 November 2025, 08:08*, vehicle *LU538UG*, pick-up: ul. 1 Maja 34, drop-off: [address requested].
* *User 2:* Ride on *14 November 2025, 07:00*, vehicle *LU418NN*, pick-up: ul. Młodzieżowa, drop-off: [address requested].

The authority relies on *Article 45(1), (3), and (6) of the Act of 16 November 2016 on the National Fiscal Administration (Ustawa o Krajowej Administracji Skarbowej)* as the legal basis.

The letter also notes that failure to provide the information could lead to a fine of up to *10,000 PLN* under *Article 45(7)* of the same Act.

h3. 2. Assessment of the legal basis

The cited article (Art. 45 of the KAS Act) regulates the powers of the National Fiscal Administration (Krajowa Administracja Skarbowa, KAS) to request information from entities, including private companies, *when performing statutory duties related to fiscal control, tax enforcement, or combating offences against public finance*.

According to Bolt’s internal lists:

* The *Act of 16 November 2016 on the National Fiscal Administration, Article 114* is listed as an *accepted legal basis* for data disclosure in Poland.
* However, *Article 45* is *not mentioned among the accepted provisions* and does not appear in the list of *not accepted* legal bases either.

After review, *Article 45* indeed empowers the KAS authorities to demand information for fiscal control purposes, including from non-taxpayers if it concerns their investigations. It is a *valid legal basis* for disclosure *when the requested data is directly relevant* to verifying compliance with tax law or identifying unlawful economic activity.

h3. 3. Scope and proportionality

The request concerns *two individual rides*, including pick-up and drop-off data, for specific timestamps and vehicles.
This is *narrow in scope* and *proportionate* to the stated purpose of tax verification. The data requested (user account details and trip metadata) are likely necessary to confirm whether the ride was properly accounted for from a tax perspective.

h3. 4. Decision

*Approved.*
The authority has cited a valid legal basis under Polish law, and the request is proportionate and specific.

h3. 5. Next steps for Risk & Compliance

* Proceed to collect:
** Passenger account information (name, phone number, email);
** Trip details (pickup, drop-off, timestamp, fare amount);
** Driver details (name, vehicle plate, tax ID if available).
* Ensure only the two rides specified in the letter are included — no historical ride data.
* Record the disclosure in the LER log with reference to the KAS legal basis (Art. 45 KAS Act).

----

In summary:
*Disclose the data.* The KAS request under *Art. 45 of the 2016 Act* constitutes a valid and proportionate fiscal authority request.

My view on each of the points:

*Continuous Program (Article I):* I agree that each policy term should stand on its own. The current setup means one issue could impact future years, which could add unnecessary exposure. Unless Aviva tied this to the commercial discount (which I do not think they have), we should push for annual agreements.

*“Follow the Fortunes” (Article IV):* This is fairly standard where the insurer handles claims. They have a vested interest in managing claims efficiently, so I’m comfortable with it as long as the gross negligence/wilful misconduct carve-out stays.

*Stacked Retentions:* I think David’s got this. It would only apply if a claim for the same occurrence crosses into a renewal year, which should be rare. For example, if a collision happened a few days before renewal but the claim was not reported until after the new policy started, Aviva could theoretically treat it as two separate policy years and apply two retentions. Therefore, we should ask Aviva to confirm its “per occurrence” to avoid any ambiguity.

*LOC Draw Trigger:* I think this could be tightened. The current language gives Aviva a bit too much flexibility. That said, given we are dealing with a large, regulated insurer, I would hope and expect them to act responsibly here. But it is probably best to clarify that draws only apply to undisputed, due amounts.

*Default Remedies (Article IX):* Agreed, this seems a bit much. It should only apply to defaults under this specific agreement, not “any other.” Otherwise, Aviva could use unrelated issues to withhold payments or cancel cover.

*Arbitration (Article VI):* This setup is standard for an insurer indemnity template. It’s not the most balanced, but I don’t see it as a deal-breaker.

*Overall:* Looks fine if we can tidy up these points, mainly the Continuous Program and LOC wording.

Until than here my first assessment:

h3. *Mietzweck*

* The Mietzweck in §1.2 closely resembles the required clause, but *should be fully aligned* with the exact Bolt wording. Small deviations can weaken Bolt's legal position in enforcing battery charging rights.


_„Die Vermietung des Lagerraums erfolgt für die Lagerung und das dauerhafte Aufladen von Lithium-lonen-Akkus für elektrische Kleinstfahrzeuge, besonders elektrische Tretroller (E-Scooter) sowie für weiteres Equipment, bspw. aber nicht abschließend Cargo-Bikes und Ort zur Aufbereitung (unter anderem Instandhaltung, Reparatur, Reinigung, Lagerung von Ersatzteilen und Einrichtung von entsprechend Reparatur- und Wartungsflächen) von E-Kleinstfahrzeugen und Büroflächen. Der Vermieter hat Kenntnis darüber, dass die dauerhafte Aufladung von Batterien für den Geschäftsbetrieb des Mieters von erheblicher Bedeutung ist.“_

h3. *Sonderkündigungsrecht*

* §2 provides some extraordinary termination rights, but the mandatory Bolt clause is only partially incorporated. The clause must be included in exact Bolt wording, particularly around power supply, 24/7 access, and regulatory constraints.

„Der Mieter kann das Mietverhältnis ohne Einhaltung einer Kündigungsfrist mit sofortiger Wirkung, insbesondere dann kündigen, wenn die Stromkapazität für seinen Geschäftsbetrieb nicht gegeben ist.
Des Weiteren steht dem Mieter ein außerordentliches Kündigungsrecht mit sofortiger Wirkung zu, wenn der Mieter das Mietobjekt rund um die Uhr nicht nutzen darf und ihm kein Zugang zu diesem Zweck gewährt wird.
Der Mieter hat auch ein Kündigungsrecht, wenn ihm behördliche Auflagen erteilt werden, die den Geschäftsbetrieb erheblich erschweren oder unmöglich machen oder die behördliche Genehmigung entzogen wird.“

h3. *Schönheitsreparaturen & Instandhaltung*

* §7.1 puts all cosmetic repairs on Bolt, capped at 5% of annual rent. Bolt policy requires this cap to be 3% max.

h3. *Rückzahlung der Sicherheitsleistung*

* §5.1 lacks a clear staged repayment mechanism (e.g., 70% after 2 months, 30% after 4 months). This should be included for Bolt compliance.

h3. *Stromkapazität*

* The agreement *does not specify available or guaranteed power capacity*. There is no clause confirming increase timing, technical feasibility, or who pays for upgrades, all required per Bolt guidelines.



* _Bestätigung durch Elektriker, dass ausreichende Stromkapazität vorhanden ist oder ausgebaut werden kann._
* _Deadline zur Herstellung ausreichender Stromversorgung: spätestens 4 Wochen nach Übergabe._
* _Kosten für Ausbau trägt der Vermieter._
* _Falls keine Erhöhung möglich: Sonderkündigungsrecht wie oben beschrieben._

h3. *Maklerkosten*

* Is there a broker involved? There is no clause clarifying broker fees or their allocation. These would need to be avoided, split or accepted.

h3. *Vertragsdauer & Verlängerung*

* Duration of 2 years + 1-year option is acceptable, but:
** No clause for special termination after 1.5 years in contracts >2 years (if term had been longer, this would be mandatory).
** Option must be exercised 6 months before end, which is reasonable.

h3. *Nebenkosten*

* Cost split per consumption is acceptable, but:
** “Sonstige Betriebskosten” open-ended clause could lead to unanticipated costs.
** Need clearer limitation or approval requirement before imposing new types of costs.
** _„Sonstige Betriebskosten (Ziff. 16 Anlage 1) bedürfen der vorherigen schriftlichen Zustimmung des Mieters.“_

+*BACKGROUND*+

* Bolt wants to collaborate with Prezzee to send vouchers to Bolt drivers.
** Prezee would allow Bolt to send Bolt-branded rewards to specified recipients.
** Bolt would need to send recipient name and contact details (email and phone) to Prezzee. We can instantly upload thousands of recipients using Prezzee’s CSV uploader.
** Bolt can keep track of who has received and opened/activated gifts sent by Prezzee.
* In particular, Bolt wants to using Prezzee in the UK for the following:
** (i) Trial of sending a small coffee voucher (£5) to each driver after their first trip, so as to increase activation rates.
** (ii) Sending thank you messages to our top 100-500 drivers in 2025.
* Timeline is ultimately unclear.

+*THOUGHTS*+

* General:
** Purpose = Marketing of Bolt’s services (as we are aiming to increase activation rates and encourage them to continue to drive) - we could aim to position it otherwise, but this is clearly the core point.
*** Legal basis = Legitimate interest (we can rely on soft opt-in, as marketing continued use of the same services).
*** This is covered in our driver privacy notice.
** Data sharing is low risk here - No need for DPIA. This is beneficial to the drivers and is unlikely to be regarded as overly invasive. No ADM.
** Main concern is how Prezzee knows which drivers have redeemed vouchers ⚠️ 
*** Email open/activation tracking falls under PECR Reg 6 (cookies & similar tech) and generally requires prior consent unless an exemption applies. We may need to disable these if drivers have not consented to them.
* Marketing:
** Third party is promoting Bolt’s services to Bolt users, but Bolt will still be considered as the sender/instigator. We can rely on soft opt-in. No need to rely on driver consent ✅ 
** Nevertheless, we must ensure the following:
*** (i) Identity of the sender (Bolt) must be clear in the marketing (this should be ok, as Prezzee allows the comms to be Bolt-branded).
*** (ii) Driver must be able to opt-out of receiving these comms (I doubt drivers would want to, but still). We may also need to share a suppression list with Prezzee, so that they can action opt-outs.
* Data Sharing:
** I cannot see any data sharing or processing agreements on Prezee’s website, let along regular terms.
** Ultimately, the data sharing is low risk here. Nevertheless, as a first port of call, we should push for an exchange agreement (or at least some data sharing terms, seeing as none appear to currently exist).
*** In terms of sending the vouchers to drivers, Prezzee seems more likely to be a processor. Bolt determines the categories of data and what they will be used for; Prezzee is merely executing these instructions. This suggests a *data processing agreement* would be appropriate.
*** However, if Prezzee uses the driver data for any of its own purposes (e.g., creating Prezzee accounts or sending its own marketing), Prezzee would also be an independent controller. It would also likely need data for fraud prevention, tax, legal requests and analytics purposes anyway, so I woukd be surprised if no IC position applied.
*** On balance, a DPA with some IC provisions would therefore be best. I will prepared one once the contractual situation is confirmed, to avid duplication of efforts.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Questions:
** When do we intend to launch this?
** What terms are we entering into with Prezzee here, if any? The website seems pretty scarce.
** What Bolt entity will be sharing this information with Prezzee? Where are the entities based?
** Will Prezzee be using the driver data for its own purposes at all? (e.g., Will it use driver contact info to send its own marketing materials? Will it create Prezzee accounts for these drivers by default?) Or can Bolt determine when such information is wiped from Prezzee’s systems?
** How does Prezzee know when a driver’s first trip is completed? Is this something we flag, or does Prezzee have access to driver trip data? Same question re our ‘top’ drivers. Same question applies to Prezzee knowing how a driver has redeemed aa voucher - does it use tracking pixels?
* Advice:
** I will need to consider the tracking pixels issue in a bit more detail.
** We should enter the DPA with Prezzee, unless an agreement already exists.
** We must ensure that the comms are Bolt-branded (“from Bolt”), and that drivers have a chance to opt-out. We may also need to share a suppression list with Prezzee, so that they can action opt-outs.

Hi, 

*Fleet Safety Incident Notifications*

Bolt should notify the fleet only once a safety complaint has been preliminarily assessed or action (e.g. suspension) has been taken.
There is no contractual obligation to notify the fleet immediately upon receipt of a complaint. However, notification can be made upon request from the fleet owner, provided:

* It does not interfere with an ongoing investigation.
* Shared information complies with UK GDPR (only necessary facts).

2. *Regulatory Reporting Obligations*

Yes, when reporting to a licensing authority, Bolt should state that the driver was operating under fleet.
This is relevant for licensing oversight and aligns with obligations under Bolt’s PHV Operator Licence (e.g. TfL). 

3. *Investigation Ownership*

Correct, safety incident investigations and any police or regulatory reporting sit with Bolt.
Bolt, as the PHV operator and platform provider, is responsible for:

* Investigating all safety incidents.
* Deciding on driver platform access.
* Escalating to police or licensing authorities as needed.

Fleets may be asked to cooperate, but the investigation lead and reporting responsibility remain with Bolt.

25W47: Bulgaria Euro Change Support

* *Done* - Bulgaria currency conversion across all eater fee types:
** Delivery fees now convert correctly for base amounts, discounted amounts in both original and discounted price fields, upsell fees, and conditional fees.
** Service fees convert for regular, discounted, and upsell scenarios.
** Small order fees convert for fee values, minimum order prices, fee caps, and all laddered thresholds, including minimum and maximum basket values and the associated fees.
** Expanded tests to cover the key scenarios mentioned above.
** Documentation was created to explain currency conversion across eater fees: [+Page: Currency Conversion Implementation in Delivery Pricing Eater Service+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENGINEERING/pages/7163347063/Currency+Conversion+Implementation+in+Delivery+Pricing+Eater+Service]
* *In Progress* - Bulgaria currency conversion across courier earnings:
** On the Pricing Courier side we still do not have a currency concept. During Croatia’s changeover a hard coded JSON was used to convert values, which we want to avoid this time. To support the January transition when BGN and EUR will run in parallel, the plan is to reuse the currency from Eater City Settings, which we already use for eater fees, and apply it to courier earnings as well.
** After researching the [+documentation+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENGINEERING/pages/6830785428/Delivery+Bulgaria+EUR+Migration] and code, the proposed solution covers both proposal and final earnings. Proposals will convert so couriers see EUR during the transition period. Final earnings will also convert so that Billing receives EUR starting on 1 Jan 2026.
** For data storage, we will store converted EUR values rather than original BGN. Between 1 - 8 Jan the city configuration will still return BGN, the converter will output EUR, and we will store EUR. After 8 Jan the city configuration will return EUR directly and we will store EUR as is. Records will carry currency set to “EUR” with total_amount in EUR.
** This aligns with downstream expectations. Billing requires EUR from 1 Jan 2026, orders will be in EUR across delivery services, and courier earnings must match the order currency. The proposal has approvals from the Billing and Logistics teams.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Hi Team,

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

# *Data retention period*


As outlined in Clause “Data Importer Obligations” of the DSA, personal data are retained only for as long as necessary to fulfil the agreed purposes. In practice, Bolt retains the Shared Personal Data only for the duration of the campaign and for a short technical period thereafter to enable reconciliation and reporting. Following this period, the data are deleted or anonymised.

Where Bolt is legally required to retain limited records for compliance, only the minimal data necessary for that purpose are kept, after which they are securely deleted.

As both parties act as independent controllers, each determines its own retention and deletion timelines in line with its internal policies and applicable data protection laws.

Looking into how to de-risk this - would it be possible to reduce the amount of email addresses to be shared during the test? 10 million records is a very large volume for an initial one-off trial and, even with a compliant EU vendor, it amplifies potential exposure in case of any mishap (wrong setup, data breach etc).

* If we can, I’d recommend starting with a smaller sample (e.g. 100-200k addresses OR choose a couple of markets only). That would still give statistically sound insights into deliverability without putting the entire rider base in scope.
* Maybe we can even choose one market with least strict privacy laws to test it out? 

A few additional points to lock down before proceeding:

# please ensure we manually delete the uploaded file immediately after we receive the verification results, rather than relying on the vendor’s 1 year auto deletion.
# confirm only the team members performing the upload can access the file and that no copy is stored locally or on shared drives.
# since we plan to mark emails as “undeliverable” in our system, make sure that classification is treated as technical quality, not a user-based decision (i.e. no profiling or behavioral interpretation).
# if this test shows value and we move toward integration or recurring use, we’ll need to switch to Bolt’s DPA template to reflect our standard safeguards (vendor audit rights, stricter sub-processor control, data breach SLAs, etc.).

+*UPDATE (21.11)*+

* *Booking reference number*: ✅ 
** Generally, passenger is not provided with a booking reference number ([link|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C080LNBM05A/p1763728639426279?thread_ts=1762876555.389819&cid=C080LNBM05A]). However, if a passenger contacted CS, apparently “_we would be able to identify the trip with minimal effort using the destination, time, and vehicle registration number_”.
*** NB. It appears that the passenger gets this information from the invoice.
** Additionally, passengers can scan a QR code to access a anonymous feedback form, and they can optionally provide their email address if they want to be contacted about the ride. Gab is separately advising on passenger feedback in Schiphol Airport on [+LSS-57296+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-57296].
*** Passengers must be able to share feedback, per tender requirements. Solution is to provide QR codes to passengers, which will take them to an anonymous survey, but passengers can provide their email address if they desire follow-ups.
*** Gab approved this as being fine, provided that we include brief disclaimer language.
*** This has been discussed with the Privacy Team - if it is a tender requirement, we should keep it. Does not necessarily clash with booking reference number (although this is potentially confusing if it is the only method for passengers to complain) ✅ 
** Overall, the key point here is that passengers should be able to complain. If we have an internal matching system that is not intrusive, then I am fine with not relying on a booking reference number specifically.
* *Location controls*: ✅ 
** It seems that location control measures are in place: “_Yes. Street hailing can only be initiated geographically on the A-line at Schiphol Airport. This limitation is enforced through the_ *_Search Category_* _settings, which prevent the feature from being used elsewhere in the Netherlands_”.
** No further comments - this is good.
* *Safety features*: ✅ 
** All safety features should be available on the driver side for NL in the context of SH ([link|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C080LNBM05A/p1763656144530859?thread_ts=1762876555.389819&cid=C080LNBM05A]).
** Based on discussions with the wider privacy team, passenger consent should not be the legal basis for any of these features (LI is always preferred). Only one would be Trusted Contact, but if the passenger does not have an account, then would not be an issue anyway. 
** As such, this is not a concern for us.
* *Disclaimer language*: ⚠️ 
** No disclaimer language is provided. Business' argument is “_since no personal data from riders is collected, a specific disclaimer is not deemed necessary_” ([here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C080LNBM05A/p1763728639426279?thread_ts=1762876555.389819&cid=C080LNBM05A]).
** I do not agree with this - pickup/destination/price (and complaints data) is still the rider’s personal data, even though the driver inputs it. I have flagged this to the business accordingly. I have also asked if there is any chance of tweaking this (?) 
* *Info in invoices*: :loading: 
** We have been provided with an example of a passenger invoice ([link|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C080LNBM05A/p1763728639426279?thread_ts=1762876555.389819&cid=C080LNBM05A]). Although a lot of the data therein is fine, some raises concerns from the driver side - VAT number, taxi license number, licence plate, email address and telephone number.
*** Also contains pickup, destination and full rider name. IMO this is fine - rider does not have the app, so this is the only record that they have of the trip.
** It could be that this is fleet-level (i.e., company details), in which case this is fine. But I am checking with the business for good measure (?) since we should not be oversharing personal data in invoices.

[~accountid:62a057c3352bf40068d0411f], it’s my understanding that the team intends to use a *US-based AI vendor* to analyse voice and video recordings for user feedback on Bolt services. After reviewing the materials, I’ve identified a number of red flags that need to be addressed before proceeding:

h3. 1. Scope of Data Processing

It’s unclear whether the processing of video recordings involves *biometric data and behavioural profiling*. Given that the tool analyses facial expressions and voice, it likely does. This would qualify as *sensitive, high-risk personal data*, requiring:

* explicit user consent,
* proper Privacy Notice disclosures, and
* a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA).

h3. 2. Privacy Notice

* *Lack of specificity about data categories*. the policy lists “name, email address, and any other data you choose to provide” which is very vague. This lack of detail is insufficient. 
* *No clarity on special categories or biometric / profiling data*. For a service analysing voice and video, there is no mention of whether biometric identifiers, profiling or facial/voice-recognition data are collected or processed. If such data is processed, it would fall under “special category” or at least “high risk” processing requiring additional safeguards (discussed above). 
* *Insufficient lawful basis detail*. The policy speaks of purposes (service, communication, security) but does not explicitly state the lawful basis for processing. 
* *No mention of transfer or localisation*. There is no explicit section on where the data is stored, whether transfers outside the EU take place, and what safeguards apply. Under GDPR, if data is transferred outside EEA, appropriate safeguards must be disclosed. 
* *Inadequate detail on retention periods*. The policy does not state how long personal data will be retained.
* *Rights explanation is minimal*. While it states rights to access, correct or delete data, it does not cover other rights such as data portability, objection to processing, restriction of processing, or the right to withdraw consent. These must be clearly explained.
* *No reference to DPIA or risk-level processing*. If the processing is high risk (voice/video analytics, possible behavioural profiling), the policy or supporting documentation should reference privacy impact assessments and mitigating steps. Nothing appears here.

Furthermore, their website indicates that GDPR compliance is still “in progress,” which is a {color:#bf2600}*significant red flag*{color}.

h3. 3. Consent Form

Please share the *consent form* - the current link appears to be broken.

h3. 4. Data Processing Agreement (DPA)

While the main Agreement references a DPA, I couldn’t locate it on their website. In any case, we should ensure the vendor signs *Bolt’s standard DPA*.

Although the vendor claims not to train their model on customer data, I couldn’t find any clauses confirming this in the Cloud Service Agreement. Is there an additional Service Agreement? Please *open a legal review ticket* as well, adding:

* T&Cs;
* Cloud Service Agreement; and
* any other related legal documents.

h3. 5. Next Steps

Before moving forward with onboarding, we must:

* clarify the *exact scope* of data processing;
* request a more detailed privacy document that addresses each of the red-flag items above;
* conduct a *DPIA*;
* update the *Privacy Notice* to include this new processing activity;
* verify that the *user consent form* complies with GDPR requirements; and
* sign *Bolt’s DPA template*.

h3. 1. Scope of Data Processing

The MSA states that “Customer Data” means any identifying information (such as name, email address, employee ID number, or _other identifying information designated by Customer_). This is very broad definition and does not mention biometric data.

The MSA does not include Data Processing Agreement. We should ensure the vendor signs *Bolt’s standard DPA*.

The vendor does not mention model training on customer data - this is problematic.

Please *open a legal review ticket* as well, adding:

* T&Cs;
* MSA; and
* any other related legal documents.

h3. 2. Consent Form

The current consent form does not indicate any AI processing and use of biometric data. 

h3. 3. Next Steps

Before moving forward with onboarding, we must:

* clarify the *exact scope* of data processing;
* conduct a *DPIA*;
* update the *Privacy Notice* to include this new processing activity;
* redraft *user consent form* to comply with GDPR requirements; and
* sign *Bolt’s DPA template*.

[@tahekai.tillo|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/U06TXKBBX08] and [@Kristjan Mereste|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/U04KBU46QS1] are in discussion internally on the better retention periods to be agreed without degrading UX functionality.

*Key Questions for Alignment*

# Should Bolt permit integrations that grant OpenAI broad access to internal Slack data, even under enterprise safeguards, or should this remain off-limits?
# Who should own and approve this decision if the business opts to proceed despite the residual risks?

Hi [~accountid:628e5c9d8026a10068b1e457] ,
I completed my review of the contract. I already accepted the changes with which we are OK with, but regarding other ones I think it is better for the team to discuss and aling.

Where we still disagree:

+*Clause 5 (fees), b)*+ - I commented that I would eliminate this. They responded that _“this is a standard clause of our main agreement with airport and cannot be eliminated. It has to remain”_. I think this is not critical, since I checked other agreements and verified that Legal always flags this clause, but they always refuse to change it & in the other cases the Team decided to proceed anyway.

+*Clause 5 (fees), e)*+ - We included a clause that stated that, if the total reel length of any digital Advertising Space increase during the Term, resulting in a reduction of our Share of Voice (SOV), the Monthly Fee for such Advertising Space shoul be adjusted downward proportionally.

They amended it to state that _“The total loop length of the Advertisements may increase or decrease during the Term. However, no automatic Monthly Fee adjustment will take place if such increase or decrease is not material so as to affect the viewing of the Advertisements, and as such it was caused directly by the actions of the Concessionaire.”_

I think this is *dangerous* because it is giving them the p*ossibility of decreasing our total loop* length. The only positive is the fact that they agreed with no automatci monthly fee adjustments in case the total loop length increases.

+*Clause 5 (fees), f) & g):*+ (regarding placement Changes and Related Costs) - I believe this one is {color:#ff5630}*critical*{color}, since it was one of the changes the team specifically instructed me to insert in the agreement.

The original clause proposed by Bolt prioritised Advertiser flexibility and cost certainty. It required the Concessionaire to (i) immediately notify Bolt of any MIA-mandated changes, (ii) offer equal or higher-value substitute placements, (iii) allow Bolt to select among these (provided they were not cheaper), (iv) maintain the original Monthly Fee even if the new space was nominally more expensive, and (v) issue an immediate pro-rata credit if no alternative was acceptable. Additionally, my version explicitly stated that such changes should not affect other placements under the contract.

In contrast, the counterproposal limits the Advertiser’s flexibility and shifts more financial exposure to Bolt. While it confirms the Monthly Fee remains unchanged for equal-value substitutions, it introduces an upward fee adjustment if a higher-value space is selected — removing the flat-rate protection in our draft. It also conditions the pro-rata refund on the absence of “suitable” alternatives without defining that threshold, which introduces ambiguity. Further, it omits the mechanism for Bolt to actively choose among substitute placements and removes the requirement to notify “immediately.”

On costs (g), both drafts align broadly in allocating reprinting/reinstallation costs to the Concessionaire in the case of MIA-imposed changes. However, the counterproposal adds a carveout: if the Concessionaire initiates the change for operational reasons (not MIA), then the cost responsibility may shift — a potential risk unless operational reasons are clearly defined.

Main points to be aware of:

* Their draft allows the Monthly Fee to increase if a higher-value alternative is chosen. This is a financial exposure Bolt had explicitly avoided.
* Discretion Over “Suitability”: The term “suitable alternative” is vague and may limit Bolt’s ability to claim a refund if they disagree with the proposed substitute.
* The counterproposal gives less agency to Bolt in selecting among alternatives.
* Reprinting Cost Carveout: The addition of an exception when the Concessionaire initiates the change (“operational reasons”) could transfer costs to Bolt unless narrowly defined.

I would *insist in maintaining our version of this clause.*


+*Our previous clause 7 and their new clause 9 (Bolt Food clause):*+ I believe it reflects what was agreed over email, but please *confirm if we are ok* with this being applied only 1 month during the entire term of the contract, instead of 1 month per year (as initially drafted).
I also added a clarification that no additional fees or charges shall apply for the use of the Advertising Spaces for this purpose.

With this I think we are ok with their change, but would feel more comfortable if they agree with my clarification paragraph.



+*On the responsibilities clause (8 in the previous version, 7 in the new version):*+

They eliminated our amendment/reference in the part where we limit our liability in claims, actions, etc, to the cases where they are _“caused by willful misconduct or negligence by the Advertiser.”_. However, I consulted other agreements and we always try to make this amendment and they never accepted, which the team has been ok with.

They did not accepted the amendment in the clause where we state that, although they are not liable for any downtime of digital medium (their part of the clause), they should be liable _“where such downtime arises from its own actions, omissions, or negligence”_ (our reference). - Again, they never accept this in the past and the team has been ok with this.

About the _“exchange of one of the Advertising Spaces mentioned above with Location Code ACCMZ1 to an alternative and more suitable advertising space”,_ they are ok with this but add that such exchange should be equal in value, and if not Bolt will have to pay the difference. 



+*Remedies clause (clause 9 in the previous version, clause 8 in the new one):*+

*a) – Delays and Substitutions*

* Our draft gives Bolt strong remedies:
** Clear thresholds: delay from their end in providing any Advertising Spaces and installation >15 days triggers substitute or credit.
** Bolt chooses substitutes from available inventory.
** Substitutions must have “comparable exposure.”
** Explicit right to credit or keep original fee without increase.
* *Their version*:
** Delay threshold is 30 days (not 15).
** Replaces “choose from inventory” with a *unilateral replacement* right by them (Bolt not consulted).
** No right to cancel or claim compensation; *credit only.*
** Adds a new clause allowing them to *leave ads visible post-term*, which could impact brand strategy if outdated materials remain displayed.

The biggest shift is from a cooperative, advertiser-choice model to a *unilateral right of the Concessionaire*, with significantly *less flexibility or control for Bolt.*

*c) & d) combined – Breach and Termination*

* *Our version* is *mutual and balanced*:
** Either party can terminate for material breach.
** Bolt can terminate if services are not delivered or substituted properly.
** Termination requires 10-day cure period.
* *Their version* is *unilateral and more aggressive*:
** Termination and remedies apply only *against Bolt* (no right for Bolt to terminate).
** Includes *liquidated damages*, late charges, interest, and deposit retention *without express cap or proportionality.*
** Allows termination *at any time and without notice* for payment default (despite mentioning 10-day cure earlier—this is contradictory).

In conclusion, their version skews *termination rights heavily in their favor* and could *expose Bolt to penalties* even for minor delays in payment.

I will wait for your comments in all these points, since I did not accepted changes in these points that are still open. Here is the [link for the agreement |https://docs.google.com/document/d/1LA0ssN4txKDBTXf6RR-Oxpl4WonCb0Jk/edit](how it is so far).

h4. *1. Employment & Liability*

h4. *Q1. What liability coverage applies if there’s an accident during the ride (personal injury, vehicle damage, third-party)?*

*A:* As far as I know, *Bolt does not have any insurance in place to cover such cases*. Separate insurance (e.g., production or event insurance) should be arranged by the organizer or production company to cover personal injury, property damage, and third-party liability during the filming.

h4. *Q2. Do we need to sign a liability waiver for creators and production crew?*

*A:* Yes, it is advisable to have a liability waiver (or include a clause in an agreement) for both:

* *Influencers/content creators*, and
* *Production crew*.

The waiver should specify that participants:

* Take part *voluntarily and at their own risk*,
* Understand the activity is *for promotional/filming purposes only*,
* Have been *advised to use appropriate safety equipment*, and
* *Hold Bolt harmless* from any liability for injury, loss, or property damage, except in cases of Bolt’s gross negligence.

h4. *Q3. Should the ride duration be clearly defined as a “simulation for promotional purposes” rather than paid courier work?*

*A:* Yes. The *ride duration and context must be clearly defined* in all documentation and communications as a *simulation for promotional purposes*, not as *paid courier work*.

This avoids:

* *Misclassification* under employment or contractor law, and
* *Confusion* regarding tax or social insurance obligations.

Participants should *not appear as active Bolt couriers* in the app, and *no payment* should be made through the platform.

h4. *2. Insurance & Road Safety*

h4. *Q4. If an influencer is officially registered as a courier and uses their own vehicle to deliver food during this filmed activation, would Bolt carry any liability in the event of an accident or damage — or would full responsibility remain with the individual (as per courier T&Cs)?*

*A:* If an influencer is *officially registered as a courier* on the Bolt Food platform and uses their *own vehicle* to perform deliveries during the filming, the *standard courier T&Cs* apply. Legally and practically, I believe it’s *safer not to register influencers as couriers*. 

h4. *3. Brand & Legal Compliance*

h4. *Q5. Are there restrictions on representing the courier uniform or brand assets (e.g., logos, bags, jackets) outside of normal operations?*

*A:* There are no specific restrictions that I am aware of, but it is recommended to *double-check with* +*Viktoriia Voskolup.*+

Hi [@alejandro.sanz|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/U02HJ2L2YE9] - for context, in principal markets:

* Bolt is the "principal" (i.e. the entity / person) that's providing the transportation services.
* Bolt is paid by the customers for the transportation services.
* Customers only have contractual relationships with Bolt.

By contract, in agency markets:

* Fleet and drivers (F&D) provide the transportation services.
* F&D are paid by the customers for the transportation services.
* Customers have contractual relationships with F&Ds and also Bolt.

On your question: Driver and fleet services providers are responsible to Bolt for any losses or costs that Bolt incurs as a result of their use of the platform. This is true for all markets, both agency and principal. If a service provider (i.e. a fleet / driver) causes an accident, they aren’t liable to Bolt for the accident itself, but they are responsible for reimbursing Bolt for any resulting costs that Bolt incurs. Bolt does not seek to regulate or impose any liability that may exist directly between customers and drivers / fleets.

In all markets, Bolt is contractually responsible to customers for any failure to comply with its obligations under our terms or local laws and regulations. Bolt is more exposed to liability for accidents in these markets, since it provides the transportation service as well as the matching service.

There are two main types of liability (though the framing differs by market): *contractual* (where there’s an agreement and something goes wrong under it) and *tortious* (where there’s no contract, such as accidents or wrongful acts). We seek to limit our liability to customers in all markets through our customer terms. 

In agency markets, Bolt may still face both contractual and tortious liability depending on the circumstances and the extent of its regulatory obligations. For example, if a driver banned by a regulator causes an accident and Bolt has allowed them to continue driving, Bolt could still be held liable. 

In practice, anyone injured in an accident involving a driver on the Bolt platform would likely bring proceedings against Bolt, the driver and any relevant fleet.

Hi Dawit, thanks for your feedback. Please see our comments in line below - we will follow up with an adjusted version shortly.

h3. *Mietzweck* {color:#36b37e}*- matches our requirements. No changes needed.*{color}

* The Mietzweck in §1.2 closely resembles the required clause, but *should be fully aligned* with the exact Bolt wording. Small deviations can weaken Bolt's legal position in enforcing battery charging rights.
* +*stated in the contract :*+ 

Die Mieträume werden zur Lagerung vermietet. Die Vermietung des Lagerraums erfolgt für die Lagerung und das dauerhafte Aufladen von Lithium-ionen-Akkus für elektrische Kleinstfahrzeuge, besonders elektrische Tretroller (E-Scooter) sowie für weiteres Equipment, bspw. aber nicht abschließend Cargo-Bikes und Ort zur Aufbereitung (unter anderem Instandhaltung, Reparatur, Reinigung, Lagerung von Ersatzteilen und Einrichtung von entsprechend Reparatur- und Wartungsflächen) von E-Kleinstfahrzeugen und Büroflächen. Der Vermieter hat Kenntnis darüber, dass die dauerhafte Aufladung von Batterien für den Geschäftsbetrieb des Mieters von erheblicher Bedeutung ist. Eine Änderung des Mietzwecks bedarf der ausdrücklichen Zustimmung des Vermieters, auf die der Mieter keinen Anspruch hat.

* +*as mandated by legal requirements :*+

_Die Vermietung des Lagerraums erfolgt für die Lagerung und das_ *_dauerhafte_* _Aufladen von Lithium-lonen-Akkus für elektrische Kleinstfahrzeuge, besonders elektrische Tretroller (E-Scooter) sowie für weiteres Equipment, bspw. aber nicht abschließend Cargo-Bikes und Ort zur Aufbereitung (unter anderem Instandhaltung, Reparatur, Reinigung, Lagerung von Ersatzteilen und Einrichtung von entsprechend Reparatur- und Wartungsflächen) von E-Kleinstfahrzeugen und Büroflächen. Der Vermieter hat Kenntnis darüber, dass die dauerhafte Aufladung von Batterien für den Geschäftsbetrieb des Mieters von erheblicher Bedeutung ist_



h3. *Sonderkündigungsrecht* {color:#36b37e}*-  matches our requirements. No changes needed.*{color}

* §2 provides some extraordinary termination rights, but the mandatory Bolt clause is only partially incorporated. The clause must be included in exact Bolt wording, particularly around power supply, 24/7 access, and regulatory constraints.
* +*stated in the contract :*+ 

Der Mieter kann das Mietverhältnis ohne Einhaltung einer Kündigungsfrist mit sofortiger Wirkung, insbesondere dann kündigen, wenn die Stromkapazität für seinen Geschäftsbetrieb nicht gegeben ist. Des Weiteren steht dem Mieter ein außerordentliches Kündigungsrecht mit sofortiger Wirkung zu, wenn der Mieter das Mietobjekt rund um die Uhr nicht nutzen darf und ihm kein Zugang zu diesem Zweck gewährt wird. Der Mieter hat auch ein Kündigungsrecht, wenn ihm behördliche Auflagen erteilt werden, die den Geschäftsbetrieb erheblich erschweren oder unmöglich machen oder die behördliche Genehmigung entzogen wird.

_Der Mieter hat auch ein Kündigungsrecht, wenn ihm behördliche Auflagen erteilt werden, die den Geschäftsbetrieb erheblich erschweren oder unmöglich machen oder die behördliche Genehmigung entzogen wird._

h3. *Schönheitsreparaturen & Instandhaltung* {color:#36b37e}*-  initially this was uncapped. We managed to negotiate it down to 5%. We are ok with the 2% delta was our target cap - annual max impact is 600€.*{color}

* §7.1 puts all cosmetic repairs on Bolt, capped at 5% of annual rent. Bolt policy requires this cap to be 3% max.

* +*stated in the contract :*+

Die Schönheitsreparaturen trägt der Mieter, soweit sie objektiv erforderlich sind. Diese Kosten sind jedoch auf maximal 5 % der jährlichen Nettomiete begrenzt.

h3. *Rückzahlung der Sicherheitsleistung -*  {color:#ff5630}*We will align this with the LL and ask for an adjustment of the contract*{color}

* §5.1 lacks a clear staged repayment mechanism (e.g., 70% after 2 months, 30% after 4 months). This should be included for Bolt compliance.

h3. *Stromkapazität -* {color:#ff5630}*We will align this with the LL and ask for an adjustment of the contract*{color}

* The agreement *does not specify available or guaranteed power capacity*. There is no clause confirming increase timing, technical feasibility, or who pays for upgrades, all required per Bolt guidelines.

h3. *Maklerkosten -* {color:#36b37e} *No Broker, we negotiate directly with LL*{color}

* Is there a broker involved? There is no clause clarifying broker fees or their allocation. These would need to be avoided, split or accepted.

h3. *Vertragsdauer & Verlängerung* {color:#36b37e}*- Since we have all relevant extraordinary termination rights, we are ok with the contract duration and extension clause.*{color}

* Duration of 2 years + 1-year option is acceptable, but:
** No clause for special termination after 1.5 years in contracts >2 years (if term had been longer, this would be mandatory).
** Option must be exercised 6 months before end, which is reasonable.



* +*stated in the contract :*+

Das Mietverhältnis beginnt voraussichtlich am 15.12.2025 und endet am 30.11.2027. Der Mieter hat das Recht auf Ausübung einer Verlängerungsoption von je einem Jahr. Die Option muss spätestens 6 Monate vor Auslaufen der regulären Mietzeit bzw. der Verlängerungszeit schriftlich ausgeübt werden. Für die Rechtzeitigkeit ist entscheidend der Zugang des Kündigungs bzw. Verlängerungsschreibens. Der Mieter kann die Mieträume bereits ab dem 01.12.2025 nutzen (Nebenkosten sind zu tragen).

h3. *Nebenkosten -* {color:#ff5630}*We will align this with the LL and ask for an adjustment of the contract*{color}

* Cost split per consumption is acceptable, but:
** “Sonstige Betriebskosten” open-ended clause could lead to unanticipated costs.
** Need clearer limitation or approval requirement before imposing new types of costs.

The user is reporting a double-charge because of incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. This typically happens in scenarios where the final amount of the transaction is not known upfront or may change.

I have checked the case and everything looks good on Bolt’s end. The pre-authorization has been released to the customer.

The user is reporting a double-charge because of incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. This typically happens in scenarios where the final amount of the transaction is not known upfront or may change.

I have checked the case and everything looks good on Bolt’s end. The pre-authorization has been released to the customer. 
You can ask the customer to reach out to their bank in order to confirm the authorized funds have been released. Their bank can locate the funds with the authorization date and amount.

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

Hello [~accountid:63da287e790148a18093a774], FO has answered with follow-up comments, I am forwarding it below:
*Labdien!*

Saistībā ar Jaunā Autoparka pārņemšanas procesu un noslēdzamo līgumu nosūtām precizējumus punktiem 2.2., 3.1. un 4.d). Šie papildinājumi ir nepieciešami, lai korekti un juridiski skaidri nodalītu atbildību starp Iepriekšējo Autoparku un Jauno Autoparku.

Mūsu mērķis nav mainīt Bolt tiesības piedzīt saistības, bet noformulēt juridisko atbildību atbilstoši faktiskajai situācijai:

* Iepriekšējais Autoparks pēc Pārņemšanas datuma faktiski nekontrolē un neekspluatē Bolt platformā esošo automašīnu.
* Jaunais Autoparks uzņemas pilnu operatīvo un finansiālo atbildību, sākot ar Pārņemšanas datumu.
* Solidārā atbildība pēc Pārņemšanas datuma radītu juridisku neskaidrību un potenciālus riskus, jo viens no subjektiem faktiski nevar ietekmēt saistību rašanos un izpildi.

Piedāvātais formulējums atbilst komerctiesību principam, ka atbildība saistāma ar reālo kontroli un saistību rašanās brīdi.

Lūdzam līguma tekstā iekļaut šādu precizētu redakciju:

*2.2.*
“No Pārņemšanas datuma Bolt vēršas tikai pret Jauno Autoparku attiecībā uz jebkādām saistībām, kas rodas pēc Pārņemšanas datuma. Iepriekšējais Autoparks netiek turēts solidāri atbildīgs par saistībām, kas rodas pēc Pārņemšanas datuma.”

*3.1.*
“Iepriekšējais Autoparks ir atbildīgs tikai par tām saistībām, kas radītas līdz Pārņemšanas datumam un ir dokumentētas un pamatotas. Sākot ar Pārņemšanas datumu, pilna atbildība par jebkurām no Līguma izrietošajām saistībām pret Bolt attiecas tikai uz Jauno Autoparku, un Iepriekšējais Autoparks netiek turēts solidāri atbildīgs.”

*4.d)*
“Bolt ir tiesības vērsties pret Jauno Autoparku līdz pilnīgai visu saistību izpildei, kas radušās pēc Pārņemšanas datuma. Bolt nav tiesību vērsties pret Iepriekšējo Autoparku par saistībām, kas rodas pēc Pārņemšanas datuma."

Esam pārliecināti, ka šāda pieeja nodrošina skaidru un paredzamu sadarbības modeli, kas ir izdevīgs un juridiski drošs visām iesaistītajām pusēm.

Ar cieņu,

+*CALL w/ ALEXANDRA & VASILE (24.11) - NOTES*+

* This initiative forms part of the broader process in RO of moving drivers from fleets to self-employment.
* Updated flows / service scope looks like the following:
** (i) FATII is essentially a driving school, which assists people with becoming ride-hailing drivers by educating them and assisting them with completing relevant documentation. Driver leads approach FATII as the first point of contact, and FATII collects their details.
** (ii) During initial contact with the driver, FATII may promote Bolt to the driver (as Bolt is offering to foot the bill for certain setup costs), as well as Pick.
** (iii) FATII shares the driver’s details with Bolt (i.e., name, contact info and city). As part of the form used to collect these details, FATII informs the driver that their data will be shared with Bolt, who will in turn reach out to the driver. Drivers have not yet signed Bolt’s T&Cs / consented to anything in our user flow.
** (iv) Bolt contacts the drivers to both: (a) promote FATII (a Bolt Rewards partner - FATII provides document renewal discount); and (b) promote Pick (another Bolt Rewards partner) by encouraging the driver to download the Pick app. Bolt will contact the drivers via live phone calls only (but may provide an electronic follow-up to drivers who are interested).
** (v) If the driver decides to sign up via Pick, Pick will help the driver set up PFA / self-employment model free of charge. Bolt also provides some sort of a discount to help with the setup - as part of this, there is some sore of exclusivity arrangement whereby the driver will then only drive for Bolt and not our competitors. For every driver that signs up via Pick, Pick pays FATII a fee (out of our scope).
* As part of Component A / the Bolt Rewards setup with FATII, Bolt is not sharing any personal data with FATII - it is still just the recipient.

+*UPDATED THOUGHTS*+

* Data Sharing:
** Bolt-FATII: No change. Bolt is still just the recipient of personal data. Current data sharing provisions ([here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/14d5_ZNXhgh7EbRoSROdvC1Ot_EjZsOMLLNwrgmrj9ts/edit?tab=t.0]) should suffice ✅ 
** Bolt-Pick: No change. DSA is already in place from [+LSS-35418+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/jira/servicedesk/projects/LSS/issue/LSS-35418] ✅ 
* Marketing:
** In terms of the marketing being done by _Bolt_, no change - FATII and Pick are both third parties to the considerations are the same ✅  As previously considered, we should be ok to contact the drivers via live telephone call without consent, 
*** However, we still need to do the following:
**** (i) We specify that it is Bolt calling, and that we got their details from FATII.
**** (ii) We do not just address marketing on the call (i.e., we address key service issues as well).
**** (iii) There is a way of these individuals to opt out of receiving these calls (in a way that is recordable / actionable on our side).
*** Also, if we intend to send electronic follow-ups to the drivers after the call, then this would be caught by DM rules and we would need to rely on consent (we cannot rly on soft opt-in). Since most of these drivers will not have yet signed up with Bolt, we will need to collect ad hoc / real-time consent. 
**** This should be requested verbally over the phone (i.e., the fact that we intend to send them follow-up materials about FATII/Pick). We should specify the mediums, as well as the right to opt-out (and how). We should then keep a careful record of these consents, as evidence 💡 
** In terms of FATII marketing Bolt’s services to driver leads, FATII is the one collecting the driver’s details in the first instance. As such, we just need to ensure the following: 💡 
*** (i) Promotional comms with the drivers should make clear that Bolt is the one providing the promotion.
*** (ii) We should ensure contractual controls are in place. I have updated the partnership agreement ([here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/14d5_ZNXhgh7EbRoSROdvC1Ot_EjZsOMLLNwrgmrj9ts/edit?tab=t.0]) accordingly.
** If Pick is in any way marketing Bolt’s services to the drivers, we will not have necessarily provided the contact details of the Bolt drivers. The drivers are signing up to the FATII app directly. In any case, the Pick DSA contains direct marketing controls, so no change is needed ✅ 
* Other:
** Given the move to self-employment context, this initiative appears to connect to [+LSS-48693+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-48693].
*** Conclusion from that ticket was that opt-in consent *_was_* required _(_“_Our understanding of the business case is that we will be actively reaching out to drivers by phone, which triggers opt-in consent rules_”), or failing that, framing the comms as operational.
*** This does not fully align with what I understand to be the legal position in RO re live marketing calls (e.g., [here|https://www.linklaters.com/insights/data-protected/data-protected---romania] and “_The undertaking of commercial communications by using_ +*_automated_*+ _calling systems_ +*_without human intervention_*+_, … is forbidden, except in cases where the subscriber concerned has previously given his/her express consent to receive such communications_”). 
*** However, that ticket does not *_fully_* align with the present case - for example, for that ticket, we were sharing personal data with third parties so that they could contact the drivers; here, we are using an outsourced processor (M+ - as discussed with Gab, we are using them as a processor and will be contracting with them). Same goes for DSA position - in that ticket, we used a full DSA because we were sharing data with third parties; that is less the case here.
*** As such, IMO, *_we could maintain the opt-out position_*. However, worth double-checking with the team for completeness first.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Check with Kostya re live calls / marketing approach, for good measure.
* Advise the following:
** Ensure that M+ makes it clear that they are calling on behalf of Bolt. We should ideally see a script of the call so that we can control it.
** If we intend to send any follow-up electronic marketing, we need to obtain verbal consent properly, record it, and action any opt-outs.

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

* The citizenship field in your system is being used to infer language ability, a new purpose not originally collected for - needs to be confirmed by the Privacy team if we are able to use these information for this purpose. 
* From a legal perspective, automatically assigning the category to Croatian citizens only (based on presumed language ability) introduces an indirect nationality-based distinction.
Even though the criterion is language, in practice it favours nationals and requires non-nationals to pass an additional test.
* Unless you can prove proportionality (i.e., the rule is necessary and there is no less restrictive way to verify language ability), this automatic citizenship-based inclusion might not stand 
* Other options are : 

a) Automatic inclusion of citizens + voluntary self-declaration for non-citizens - If repeated rider feedback notes “communication issues,” driver could lose access after review.

b) Voluntary self-declaration for all drivers (“I confirm I speak Croatian fluently”) - If repeated rider feedback notes “communication issues,” driver could lose access after review.

c) Short automatic in-app test or phone interview for all interested drivers

*Findings:*

* *Financial Statements:* Contain only corporate financial results and standard disclosures. The only personal data included are the names of directors, legal representatives, and the auditor.

* *Data Minimization:* Access is limited to targeted data strictly required for audit purposes.{quote}

Hi Team,

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

Marketing wants to impersonate living personality Robert Ten Brink, TV host of Dutch show “All. You need is love” and also call the campaign “All you need is Bolt”.So we don't make a direct reference. We don't name the show, but we are imitating the original presenter.

The risk that he will ask to delete the video or ask for compensation for unauthorised usage of his character exists. We could also ask for official approval of Robert Ten Brink. But he may demand fees for using of the character.

*Possible consequences:* Bolt may face with *cease and desist letter*, *claim for reputational damages, claim about breach of right to privacy* from the TV host.

[https://share.google/A7bVIVZikgtsxNazo|https://share.google/A7bVIVZikgtsxNazo|smart-link]  

Original: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2kszS2nOrWU|https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2kszS2nOrWU|smart-link] 

Imitator: [https://www.instagram.com/p/C1HD2w_tvem/|https://www.instagram.com/p/C1HD2w_tvem/|smart-link] 

*Marketing should take into account the following:* 

* No logos of the TV show, no real names of TV host. 
* No impersonalisation of moves specific to the person (e.g. gestures) - specific for German law but I advise to stick to this for other markets, as well 

*_Here we should also refer to the assessment we did for Angela Merkel case for Germany._* 

*Germany* *case law that was revenant for Angela Merkel case.* 

There is extensive case law regarding the use of celebrity images (or of their lookalikes) in advertising.

*I.* The Regional Court of Cologne has ruled that advertising with a *Jogi Löw* (former coach of the German national football team) *lookalike* violates the general right of personality and the right to his own image
“The degree of similarity between the two persons and thus the differences in the external appearance of the two persons and with regard to their language habits for example, (…), are irrelevant in the end, because it is precisely a matter of making the plaintiff’s advertising value fruitful by attracting attention to the goods offered by the defendant. For this purpose, *_it is sufficient if a similarity between the two persons, given at first glance, creates the - albeit possibly only fleeting - idea that the person shown is the prominent applicant._*” (Regional Court of Cologne, decision of 01.06.2021, 28 O 218/21).

*II.*  In another case, the Higher Regional Court of Cologne has ruled on an advertising video of a furniture store using images of a *TV host lookalike*. The commercials showed scenes from a television quiz show in which a double played a host, which the court classified as a violation of the right to one’s own image. The court stated that in the case of advertising with predominantly commercial interests, the general right of personality of the person depicted without his consent is usually affected. “*This is because it is an essential part of the general right of personality to decide for oneself whether and in what way one’s own image should be made available for advertising purposes.* However, the focus is on the fact that the use of an image exploits the image or advertising value of the person depicted and gives the impression that the person depicted identifies with the advertised product, recommends it or praises it.” (OLG Cologne, judgement of 6 March 2014 - 15 U 133/13).

Hi Team,

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten
