[~accountid:5eb363355862510b794e3507] was in TUV for bike UL2849 testing {{2025-11-24}}. We encountered a negative current problem during the cutoff at max speed test.

*Cutoff at max speed test：*

_How does the lab test:_

_Pedaling until the speed reaches 1.25 times the maximum speed, and when the speed exceeds 20MPH, the current of the motor phase needs to be 0._

* Due to the regen brake, the oscilloscope measured negative current.
* Asked Genfo to make an FW to close the regen brake， but the negative current is still there.
* Then made a new FW with max speed 25km/h（15.53mph) to diagnose where the negative current is coming from.  When the speed is in 15~20mph, no negative current. But when the speed exceeds 20MPH, the negative current appears.

From tests, we believe that the problem is from the motor itself, the motor does not hava a clutch, when the pedaling speed exceeds its maximum designed speed of the motor, it will produce negative current.

Because this is the first time for TUV testing a motor without a clutch， and the standard only specifies when the pedaling assist stops, the current needs to be reduced to no-load current.

I have challenged the interpretation of the standards, and the laboratory engineers have agreed to seek approval from their leaders tomorrow and provide a response. I have a 95% confidence in convincing their leaders.

These problems have been discussed with [~accountid:6215e9f275803500683497d5] today.

[~accountid:712020:41e1c836-f756-4994-b3dc-d4c2dda9e358] Our feedback to the campaign idea in general is the following:

*Conclusion:* We advise against using the campaign title “All You Need is Bolt” in combination with imitation of Robert Ten Brink, the host of _“All You Need is Love”,_ without his consent.

*Background*
The marketing team has proposed a campaign titled *“All You Need is Bolt”*, inspired by the Dutch television show _“All You Need is Love”_, hosted by Robert Ten Brink. The proposed campaign would involve an imitation of the TV show host’s persona and presentation style for promotional purposes.

*Legal Assessment*
While parody and humorous impersonation can sometimes fall under exceptions such as fair use, these typically apply to non-commercial or editorial contexts. In this case, the proposed use is for commercial advertising, promoting Bolt’s services, and would therefore be considered a commercial exploitation of another person’s image and persona.

Even though we are not using the original show title verbatim, the campaign name “All You Need is Bolt” is highly reminiscent of _“All You Need is Love”_, and the impersonation of the recognizable TV host could create a strong association or confusion with the existing show and its host. This increases the likelihood of a claim of *unauthorized use of likeness* or *misappropriation of personality*.

*Risks Identified*

# *Cease and desist letter* – The host or rights holders of the TV show may request the immediate removal of all campaign materials.
# *Claim for compensation* – Robert Ten Brink could demand financial compensation for the unauthorized commercial use of his likeness or character.
# *Right to privacy / personality rights claim* – The host may claim that his personal rights have been infringed.
# *Reputational harm* – The association between Bolt and the show without authorization could lead to negative press coverage or public criticism.

*Possible Mitigation*

* *Seek prior approval or license*: Approach Robert Ten Brink (or his representatives) for official consent to use his likeness or character. However, it is likely that he would request a fee or impose conditions on the campaign’s content and distribution.
* *Adjust campaign concept*: To reduce legal and reputational exposure, it is strongly recommended to develop a more neutral campaign name and creative approach, avoiding any direct or implied reference to the TV show or its host.

This advice is based on our experience in similar matters across various EU countries. However, a Dutch law expert may have a different opinion depending on local laws and court practice. If you would like to obtain a local legal opinion, please let us know - [~accountid:712020:8fd75aa8-dcfb-42ad-93ab-53900ee4c301] has suitable contacts who can assist with this question.

We’re comfortable proceeding with this risk profile for introducing the Priority Support Fee (PSF) in Cyprus. 

In summary: There's no explicit legal restriction, though the primary risk involves potential interpretation by the Road Transport Authority as an unlawful fare supplement. 

To mitigate this, the PSF must be:

* Presented as a separate, platform-level charge (not part of the fare).
* Clearly itemised in the app and fully transparent before booking.
* Retained by Bolt (not drivers/fleets) and not impact driver pay or regulated fares.
* Linked to non-transport services (e.g., business support).

Outside counsel also endorsed the proposed T&Cs language.

----

Considering that the minivans currently do not have a taxi license, the described services fall under the category of *irregular passenger transport services*, meaning passenger transport services carried out by a carrier on the basis of a contract (order) concluded with the customer and not related to a regular transport service (governed, among others, by Articles 4.0.4 and 21-1.2 of the Law “On Automobile Transport” dated 01.04.2008, hereinafter the “*Law on Automobile Transport*”, and Article 8.1-1 of the Rules “On the carriage of passengers and luggage by automobile transport” dated 17.09.2009, hereinafter the “*Rules*”). 

# *Documentation*

For the carrying out of *irregular passenger transport services* such as proposed minivan services the following documents must be obtained from AYNA (Azerbaijan Land Transport Agency) for each vehicle:

* *Permit* for domestic charter transportation _(ölkədaxili sifarişli daşımalara buraxılış vəsiqəsi)_, (Articles 4.0.7 and 13.1.2 of the Law on Automobile Transport, and Clause 33 of Annex 3 of the Law of Azerbaijan “On Licenses and Permits dated 15.03.2016), and
* *Registration card* _(buraxılış kartı)_ (Article 1.0.36 of the Law on Automobile Transport).

Obtaining the above documents is free of charge.

# *Special form*

Upon obtaining these documents, a special form (formulyar) must be completed (information regarding the vehicle, driver, passengers, transportation time etc.) for the provision of minivan services through the electronic system of AYNA (Article 22.4 of the Law on Automobile Transport, and Articles 8.4 and 8.5-1 of the Rules).

Linked please find the website for completing the special form for carriers in Azerbaijani - [https://e-xidmet.ayna.gov.az|https://e-xidmet.ayna.gov.az|smart-link].

# *The risks of non-compliance*

The risk of enforcement in case of non-compliance is high, and it may result in the following:

+Administrative liability+

Article 324 of the Code of Administrative Offences

* The organization of luggage and irregular passenger transportation by a carrier without a permit entails a fine of up to AZN 600 for officials and AZN 2,400 for legal entities.
* The organization of luggage and irregular passenger transportation by a carrier without a registration card entails a fine of up to AZN 100.

Article 322 of the Code of Administrative Offences

* The carrying out of irregular passenger transportation (excluding passenger transportation by taxi cars) without completing the special form entails a fine of AZN 50.

+Liquidation of the company+

Operating without a special permit or license constitutes grounds for the liquidation of the company by court decision.(Article 59.2.3 of the Civil Code of Azerbaijan)



*To summarize -* the Law on Automobile Transport respectively categorizes the passengers and luggage transportation services (Article 4), taking into account all possible scenarios. *Therefore, there is no basis for arguing that this service does not fall under the described irregular passenger transport services* *category.*

Hi [~accountid:712020:e04282ea-9d2c-4f81-8507-cea4db4cd1b9] ! Thank you for raising this question 🙏 

FOs and Drivers are considered as independent data controller under applicable data protection regulations. This means that they are responsible for ensuring that any recording or sharing of passenger data complies with the GDPR and local legislation, particularly regarding transparency, consent, and lawful processing.


If they use cameras or other recording devices aboard their vehicle, they have to ensure the following - which you could remind them of at e.g. Driver Engagement Center appointments:

* passengers are clearly informed through visible notices that a recording is taking place;
* the purpose, controller details, data retention period, and a reference to a privacy notice are made available; and
* any processing of recordings is conducted lawfully and securely.

The important point here is that since Bolt and those FOs/Drivers are independent controllers, and that Bolt does not provide, install or control any recording devices, and we do not have access to or the ability to remove or delete such content, our involvement is very limited. The FOs/Drivers remain accountable for ensuring compliance with data protection law and for any breaches arising from their actions on this front.

In short: they can use cameras, with or without sound, facing whichever way they want -  Bolt does not encourage nor discourage it, we are completely separate from any decision on that front and should not be influencing them in one way or another.

Please note that a new feature will be rolled out soon, which will enable drivers to indicate to riders that they use CCTV via their profile - more information can be found [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C02CUF8CFCZ/p1763988822063919].

When a *KYC (Know Your Customer) request* is raised, the following process typically occurs:

# *Submission & Initial Review*
The request is logged in the system, and the customer’s details (e.g., ID documents, address proof, business registration) are submitted for verification.
# *Document Verification*
The compliance or verification team reviews the submitted documents. Automated tools may also check the authenticity of IDs, match names, and validate against external databases (like sanctions or PEP lists).
# *Risk Assessment*
Based on the customer’s profile, activity, and jurisdiction, the system or team assigns a risk level (low, medium, or high).
# *Approval or Escalation*
#* If everything is in order, the KYC request is *approved*, and the customer status is updated to “Verified.”
#* If issues are found (e.g., expired documents, mismatched data), the request is *escalated* for manual review or clarification from the customer.
# *Completion Notification*
The requester or relevant team receives a notification that the KYC process is complete, along with the outcome (approved, rejected, or pending more info).

+*BACKGROUND*+

* Bolt is piloting a holistic improvement of high-value categories (Comfort, Premium, XL) by setting higher standards for driver performance, vehicle quality, and rider experience. 
* The project involves the following:
** (1) *Dual eligibility*: In addition to vehicle type, drivers will only be able to use these categories if they meet certain quality metrics (i.e., rating, acceptance rate, drive score, finished orders and completion rate) - see [here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1hvRNiMbdcTxpScxQY_zBvC8emnojEKLLPiPH0_5VIYU/edit?tab=t.7uo6s5eia9mt].
** (2) *Category access filters*: Drivers can be excluded based on automatic and manual mechanisms.
** (3) *Driver comms*: Improved comms (via email) about entry, removal and eligibility re premium categories- see [here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Bis7McoKlIygoNdMn2TdjmjH9nZLkgca0VeaBeL_WVU/edit?tab=t.0].
** (4) *Quality inspections*: Ongoing review of premium vehicles via photo submissions (in the short term, collecting photos from drivers in a local Sharepoint folder; in longer term, using a full solution), surveys (of rider sentiment) and mystery shopping (i.e., someone taking rides to check).
** (5) *Rider-facing improvements*: New category branding to make categories clearer, ensuring that vehicle matches as advertised, longer vehicle wait times, add-ons for ride categories (rather than separate categories for pets etc.), professional driver standards / ability to select car conditions and amenities, and in-app feedback loops.
* The pilot is coordinated locally in 10 cities including: *Riga, Tallinn, Baku, Prague, Warsaw, Bucharest, Stockholm, Valletta, Paris, Lisbon, Cape Town, Madrid, London.* The duration of the pilot will be around *8 - 12 weeks*.
** The current ticket is relevant to the UK. However, no-one from Privacy has been looped in for the other countries, so worth doing a holistic review.
** It appears that the project timeline is [here|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1hJPvuM-LXogi9UiNkqFTjk_DF2hQUO-lIhzOXD3CJ4c/edit?gid=160066481#gid=160066481].
* Central Legal has already reviewed (here), and their main conclusions are as follows:
** Performance KPIs are risky from a reclass POV - see [here|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1yvdOuX3nF48XG0o8YDGArjobHYR60BVvOR_dZp-AkQU/edit?gid=0#gid=0].
*** Acceptance Rate and Driver Score are particularly tricky. Recommended to rely on rating, cancellation rate and number of finished orders in high-risk markets (i.e., only stick to strictly necessary KPIs).
*** Also, individual driver ratings are not visible to drivers, and so using them as a metric for eligibility is likely to cause concerns. External comms should instead focus on ‘rider complaints’.
** Mandatory dress codes and vehicle amenities (paid for by _Bolt_) also introduce reclass risk, as they create the impression of employment-like control.
** Warning comms should contain clear explanations of why drivers are being removed from the category.
*** Central Legal flagged that all comms should be reviewed by them first.
** Drivers should have a 48-hour window in which to appeal being excluded from a category.
*** If warning comms are not used before removing a driver, there should be a comprehensive and structured customer support process is put in place to handle appeals and questions.

+*ANALYSIS*+

* *EU Privacy Analysis*: [+*LINK*+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/14CmJpL-aSKQ82zKFbWsw_Xszjh9uzeEkOMkxvRd3gzI/edit?tab=t.0]
* *Monitoring driver KPIs to determine premium category eligibility*: {color:#6554c0}*High risk*{color}
** We are not collecting any new, nor particularly sensitive data here. 
*** However, we can still push for better {color:#36b37e}*data minimisation*{color} - if acceptance rate and driver score are not necessary, then drop them 💡 
** If push comes to shove, we can argue that this is covered in the privacy notice ('customising transportation services'), and that we are doing so based on a mixture of contractual necessity and legitimate interest.
*** Worth asking {color:#4c9aff}*if this is covered anywhere in our T&Cs*{color} (?) Impacts legal basis, transparency and possible need for a LIA.
** However, this is partially {color:#ff5630}*invisible processing*{color} ⚠️ 
*** The driver privacy notice does not make it explicitly clear that we monitor KPIs like this to determine eligibility for premium categories. Drivers would not necessarily expect that we do in any case, and so there is a noticeable transparency gap here.
*** It seems unlikely that we will be updating the privacy notices globally soon. We can either: (i) {color:#36b37e}*update the driver privacy notice*{color} to reflect this; and/or (ii) {color:#36b37e}*publish articles / blog posts / driver comms*{color} informing drivers about this 💡 
** Given that the processing is invisible, looks like scoring, flirts with ADM and is potentially exclusionary, it is worth conducting a {color:#ff5630}*DPIA*{color} ⚠️ 
*** This argument is only straightened by the fact that this is being proposed globally, not just in the UK. Drivers are likely to care about this, and so we need to make sure that the correct documentation is in place.
** If monitoring KPIs and exclusion from the categories is fully automated, there is technically an ADM{color:#ff5630} {color}risk here, as it prevents drivers from earning a living on the premium categories.
*** However, our position can be that A22 is not triggered here. As discussed with Gab, category allocation does not fall under A22. Although this project involves profiling and measuring KPIs, we can still argue that it does not produce a significant effect, as (i) drivers can still use other categories; and (ii) if the driver later meets the KPIs, they regain access to the premium categories.
*** Worth asking more about automation of {color:#4c9aff}*category access filters*{color}, as well as whether{color:#4c9aff} {color}{color:#4c9aff}*_permanent_* {color}{color:#4c9aff}*banning takes place*{color} (?) 
*** To avoid accusations of ADM, we should: (i) ensure a {color:#36b37e}*human review / appeals process*{color} before exclusion; (ii) {color:#36b37e}*clearly document and explain*{color} how exclusion process and review process works; (iii) ensure that {color:#36b37e}*comms are clear*{color} on why a driver has been excluded; and (iv) ensure the {color:#36b37e}*system is robust*{color} and does not result in errors 💡 
** In terms of exercising DSRRs:
*** We would need to provide the metrics in response to a DSAR - not necessarily an issue. However, drivers may ask for information on the scoring metrics - assuming that the business does not want to share this in detail, blog posts might be useful.
*** If relying on LI, drivers could object, but we can push back on overriding compelling grounds.
** No obvious third-party sharing.
* *Driver comms*: {color:#6554c0}*High risk*{color}
** As mention above, core concern here is making sure that we are: (i) as detailed / open as possible in comms about eligibility and removals; and (ii) we provide this information to drivers in a timely and user-friendly manner (e.g., warnings) 💡 
*** It looks like drivers will be sent warnings ([here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Bis7McoKlIygoNdMn2TdjmjH9nZLkgca0VeaBeL_WVU/edit?tab=t.4ntyngmbuskj]). Worth asking {color:#4c9aff}*how far in advance and how frequently*{color} drivers will be warned (?) 
** Currently, the eligibility draft ([here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Bis7McoKlIygoNdMn2TdjmjH9nZLkgca0VeaBeL_WVU/edit?tab=t.0]) contain various gaps that could do with plugging, in particular: ⚠️

Here are some guidelines about what you should and should not say in the interview questions. 

# *Keep it neutral and flexible*

* Say “using the Bolt app” instead of “working for Bolt.”
* Ask about what drivers choose to do, not what they must do.
* Focus on experience and choices, not on “rules” or “requirements.”

# *Avoid employment-style terms*

* Don’t use words like work, job, shift, salary, wage, pay, full-time, part-time, manager, team.These suggest employment rather than independent driving.

# *Safer alternatives*

* “How many hours do you usually choose to drive?” (not “work each week”)
* “When do you usually go online?” (not “start your shift”)
* “What factors influence your earnings?” (not “how much do you earn”)
* “What made you decide to start driving with Bolt?” (not “take this job”)
* “How do you receive payments for trips you complete?” (not “how does Bolt pay you?”)

# *Use choice and independence language*

Highlight driver control:

* “You decide when and where to drive.”
* “You choose how to plan your time.”
* “You manage your own experience on the platform.”

# *Avoid promises or guarantees*

* Never imply fixed income, set targets, or minimum earnings. Instead, focus on what helps influence earnings (location, time of day, etc.).

Well, the driver doesn’t owe anything in total so there is nothing to invoice. We deduct compensations/bonuses from total commission so if there are more bonuses than commission, there’s nothing to charge. In the current example: 134.36€ (commission) - 100€ (earning_campaign_bonus) - 36.85€ (earning_campaign_bonus) - 9.30€ (earning_cash_discount_netted) - 12.40€ (earning_in_app_discount_netted) = -24.19€ → the driver doesn’t owe Bolt anything, so there’s nothing to invoice. 

So yes, we can’t provide an invoice for this. 🙂

Hi team, 

Thank you for escalating! 
The customer has a negative balance due to a technical issue from Bolt’s end. 

This bug happens with Alternative Payment methods (APMs). APMs don’t have dual messaging — Authorization + Capture. They just have the capture. 
If the payment amount is lower than the captured amount then Bolt will automatically refund the difference. 

In this case the capture was for 29.46 PLN, but order price was just 9.5 PLN (cancellation fee). 
This triggered an automatic refund for 19.96 PLN. 

Now when the full refund for 9.5 PLN was issued then it triggered the bug/discrepancy between how the refund was recorded on the payment vs order. The full refund for payment was 29.46 PLN. However, for the order the full refund is 9.5 PLN. 

29.46 PLN - 9.5 PLN = 19.96 PLN. 

How to solve the issue for the customer? 
The customers balance cannot be amended. The only way we can solve the issue for the customer is to issue a Bolt Balance refund. 
Unfortunately, the customer payments team doesn’t have any accesses to issue refunds to to BB. 

Could you please issue a Bolt Balance refund for the customer for 19.96 PLN? You might not be able to issue the refund from the original order as the “refund has already been issued”. Could you please try to issue the refund from customers other recent orders? If you have any issues you might want to check with your team lead as they have higher permissions to refund from old orders. 

Please note that this has been escalated to payment engineers to fix here.

Hi [~accountid:6102798ec51f3a0069a7b366], thanks for reporting.

We decided to reject this ticket.

* The current behaviour is _similar_ to the regular MQ publishers in comp tests (e.g. for SQS): if a single service is both the publisher _and_ consumer, it does _not_ mean that in a test where an event is published, the subscriber will be automatically triggered as well. One has to _explicitly_ mock receiving a message on the subscriber input and then verify the expected effects of receiving the message. This can already be done for CDC publishers, and we’d like to keep the experience consistent.
* There are very few services subscribing to the CDC publishers, which does not indicate high demand for any optimisations in this area.

Hi Team,

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

To whom it may concern,

We refer to our previous correspondence dated [insert date when the original letter was sent], in which we raised a formal dispute regarding your damage claim for vehicle registration DK DT16249 under rental agreement 999076643.

To date, we have not received any substantive response addressing the points raised in that letter. Instead, on 21 November 2025, we received your follow-up email threatening referral of the matter to a collection agency. Given that the matter remains formally disputed, any referral to a collection agency would be premature and inappropriate.

Please note that Bolt formally contests the validity of this invoice and does not accept liability for the claimed amount. As outlined below (and previously), there is no legal or factual basis for the application of the full repair cost or for the removal of the agreed excess protection.

# +*Dispute of Gross Negligence Classification:*+

Based on the information available and the damage shown in the photos, it appears the driver may have misjudged the vehicle’s clearance and struck an overhead structure at low speed. The damage appears to be limited to the roof panel, with no indication of structural damage, third-party involvement, or any police report or formal determination by the authorities that reckless driving occurred.

We note that the rental agreement references Danish Law L534 (Section 133a of the Road Traffic Act) regarding reckless driving. However, this legislation is aimed at addressing extreme high-risk behaviours, such as:

* Driving over 200 km/h
* Speeding by more than 100% (above 100 km/h)
* Driving under the influence (BAC > 2.0)
* Street racing or deliberately endangering others

For reference: [ |https://www.retsinformation.dk/eli/lta/2021/534][+Lov nr. 534 af 27. marts 2021 – Danish Road Traffic Act (Section 133a)+|https://www.retsinformation.dk/eli/lta/2021/534]

There appears to be no evidence that any of these conditions apply in this case, nor has there been any assessment by Danish authorities confirming a violation of this law. As such, the reference to L534 appears to be a contractual interpretation rather than a legal one, and we do not believe this justifies the removal of the excess protection.

# +*Request for Full Cost Breakdown:*+

The amount claimed (DKK 92,603.97) appears disproportionately high for the visible level of damage. Therefore, before any liability is accepted or payment is considered by us in full or part thereof, we request the following:

* A detailed, itemised invoice showing parts, labour, admin, and any loss-of-use costs
* Confirmation of the repair strategy (e.g. full panel replacement vs. repair)
* Evidence of any third-party vendor quotes, where applicable
* A breakdown of how the figure was calculated relative to AVIS’s standard damage estimation process

# +*Request for Cost Reduction or Settlement Terms:*+

We are open to resolving this constructively and ask that AVIS reconsider the charge in light of the points raised above. Given the low-speed nature of the incident, the lack of third-party involvement, and the apparent overreach in applying L534, we believe a more proportionate response would be appropriate.

We would welcome:

* A reassessment of the charge
* A possible reduction
* And/or application of the original deductible amount, as agreed in the rental contract.

We trust that AVIS, as a long-established mobility provider, will take a fair and reasonable approach when evaluating this matter.

#  *Response template (Safety)* -> [Link|https://drive.google.com/drive/u/0/folders/1-8B314hU2zmT2G1NHAASKXolVGHnmRyV] (In progress).

+*BACKGROUND*+

* Main Slack channel is here: [#temp-ee-airport-kiosk|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C099SBLJ42E]
* We are contracting with Tapbox as the relevant service provider.
* Whether we use a DSA or a DPA depends on whether Tapbox will be using the data for its own purposes, or strictly on our instructions.
** Tom Bishop confirmed Tapbox “_should only be doing it on Bolts instructions_” ([+link+|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C099SBLJ42E/p1761235829532299?thread_ts=1760345585.470629&cid=C099SBLJ42E]) - this suggests a [DPA|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ezFeNGwxwQXdST451Fb_OiDlOaYOJybJ3aMGguNWpF0/edit?tab=t.0] would be better. I falgged the DPA draft last month and said I could incorporate it into the agreement once the agreement is more developed.
** However, it seems likely that we are using the API Integration model., which could instead suggest a DSA.
*** With Virtua, this is certainly the case, even though the model is ill-fitting. For Virtua, I prepared our standard DSA ([+link+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1O7UQJzQAACEujR3XSiGaAr8_vPxC3pGZDh06UhCcmX4/edit?tab=t.0]), with some minor tweaks to incorporate the key provisions of the API DSA.
*** In Tanzania, Aleks also used our standard DSA ([+LSS-56179+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-56179]), so worth keeping that in mind as well.

+*UPDATE (25.11)*+

* Central stakeholders are currently working on the Integration Agreement ([link|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C099SBLJ42E/p1763646008211199?thread_ts=1763553427.491829&cid=C099SBLJ42E]).
** This is the Virtua agreement - API Integration, with a DSA incorporated. Given the ill-fitting model, we can proceed with the DSA for now. It is more important to have contractual protections in place in some form - we have already flagged the risks.
* Otherwise, awaiting update re incorporation of Tapbox T&Cs / PP into the order flow.
** NB. Inclusion of the booking ID in the receipt was suggested to the TapBox team in June ([here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C08C50GNLHE/p1750143183348209]). It looks like this is being implemented.
** Yesterday, I was added to a Slack thread with Tapbox representatives for Latvia ([link|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C08C50GNLHE]- created in Feb 2025). Points of note are as follows:
*** Order flow states “_By booking, you agree with TapBx/Bolt’s terms and privacy policy_”.
**** On 12 June, request was to remove the checkbox next to the T&Cs, as “_we’ve decided not to use it_” ([link|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C08C50GNLHE/p1749731370229719]).
**** However, on 13 November, Tapbox suggested that passengers _would_ be accepted TapBox’s T&Cs (in addition to Bolt’s) ([here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C08C50GNLHE/p1763060922425889?thread_ts=1763034470.610829&cid=C08C50GNLHE]).
**** TapBox T&Cs are [here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1dI37prF5cKji8aPpJ3U4vKzz3b0PN7eCmCT97Jm1_kQ/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.6jqecfb9kch1]. Extremely minimal (mostly compliance with laws), but Clause 4 effectively functions as TapBox’s privacy notice. Does not comment on controller vs processor. In terms of liability, states that TapBox is jointly responsible for ensuring a taxi is dispatched.
*** *CONCLUSION*: Tapbox’s T&Cs / ‘privacy policy’ do not really strengthen either the agreement for IC or the argument for C-P. On balance, I think this setup looks more like controller-processor; however, given that: (i) we are adopting the (ill-fitting) API integration setup (which favours C2C, and a DSA has been incorporated into it); (ii) Tapbox is an independent collector of passenger fares (see [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C097B56T3QR/p1764071156695989]), and so will be doing at least some IC activities anyway; (iii) a DSA has already been used in other countries; and (iv) there is pressure from the business to execute (and we need to have some contractual protections in place), we can *stick with the DSA approach*.
* NEXT STEPS:
** For good measure, I am double-checking if TapBox stores data on its own systems for any purposes, as well as whether Bolt’sPN is included anywhere. This would further justify DSA approach ([link|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C08C50GNLHE/p1764067722103239?thread_ts=1763034470.610829&cid=C08C50GNLHE]).

h3. *💡 Proposal*

* Adding a timeframe filter to the PDE tool
* Restricted permissions for in-house CS (to use only timeframe filtering without the possibility to download all data held about a user)

+Why we'd like to leverage the PDE Tool for CS to extract user data for law enforcement?+

All the required plugins are already consolidated in one place, and the data can be extracted without exposing sensitive or internal information that might be unintentionally shared through other tools. For instance, if an agent currently uses the order export tool to pull data on a specific rider, they would also receive the driver’s personal details for each order. 

+Why we'd like to include a timeframe filter for the PDE Tool?+

Law enforcement requests are always tied to a specific timeframe (a defined set of dates), so it’s important that we limit the data shared to only what is necessary. Instead of CS downloading entire datasets (all orders, all communications, all transactions) and then manually excluding irrelevant information, a process that is both inefficient and prone to human error, CS would simply enter the user ID, specify the relevant timeframe, select the necessary plugins, and download the export from the PDE Tool. Timeframe filtering would apply to the plugins mentioned *below*, while others (such as user profile and security) would continue to be downloaded in full as usual.

*🚗 Rider:*

* Communications
* Customer support
* User billing
* User carsharing rental details
* User Orders

🥡🥕 *Eater:*

* Communications
* Customer support
* User billing
* User Orders

*🚗* *Partner (Driver):*

* Communications
* Customer support
* Driver billing
* Driver documents (?)
* Driver order history
* Driver telemetry data 
* State log

🥡🥕 *Partner (Courier):*

* Communications
* Courier order history
* Courier invoicing reports
* Customer support

----

h3. *📊 Impact*

[+PDE Tool - Feature Requests - Data+|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/16fVr0u-MzYxnTLRQCvtGhUzQA8d2DoB9xzckl0vI3ZQ/edit?gid=1407908205#gid=1407908205] - second tab

* On average, CS receive 800 requests a month regarding plugins mentioned under *💡 Proposal* (as these datapoints are time-consuming to compile). Total number of monthly law enforcement requests is much higher. 
* The extraction time can vary depending on the vertical (e.g. in delivery there is no order export tool at all), what specific information is being requested, and about how many users / orders. However, if I were to give some kind of rough estimate, I'd go with 30-45 minutes.
* Hourly rate: €13,74/hour. That is the lowest hourly rate within CS Privacy. I don’t have an overview of regular in-house CS specialists salaries, however, their salary shouldn't exceed this amount. 

800 requests * 30 min = 400 hours

400 * 13,74 = 5496

~65k euro per year

----

h3. *🚀 Goals of the implementation*

*✅* - Reduce the number of tools (and devs teams) CS needs to involve to download basic user data for law enforcement requests

*✅* - Implement a consistent approach for data extraction that can be applied to all verticals

*✅* - Improved efficiency and speed 

✅ - Reduced human errors 

✅ - CSPC would no longer need to support high-volume requests

+*Summary of Developments After the Precautionary Measures*+
After the Tribunal Superior de Justicia de Galicia granted precautionary measures suspending the enforcement of Articles *20.2*, *70.6*, and *73* of the A Coruña Sustainable Mobility Ordinance, the *City of A Coruña* filed a request for clarification of the order (not a formal appeal).
The City argued that the suspension *should not include Article 73*, which regulates the *legal framework for the activity of vehicle rental with driver (VTCs).*


*Ecija’s lawyers*, representing Enol Mobility, *opposed* the clarification request, contending that the City was not seeking a true clarification under Articles *214 and 215* of the Civil Procedure Act (_Ley de Enjuiciamiento Civil_), but rather attempting to have the court *revisit the substance (“fondo del asunto”)* of the decision already made.


Despite this opposition, the Court *admitted the City’s request* and, by order of *14 November 2025*, *confirmed the precautionary suspension* only for *Articles 20.2 and 70.6*, *excluding Article 73* from its scope.

+*Key Legal Reference*+

* *Article 73 of the Mobility Ordinance*: Establishes the *regulatory regime for VTC activity* in the municipality, i.e., conditions and limits for the operation of chauffeur-driven rental vehicles.



*In summary:* The City of A Coruña requested clarification, arguing that Article 73 should not be suspended; Ecija (for Enol) opposed, claiming it was an attempt to alter the original ruling; however, the Court admitted the clarification and limited the precautionary suspension to Articles *20.2* and *70.6*, effectively *lifting it for Article 73.*

It is acceptable to include the €1 fee in the passenger-facing disclaimer, provided that:

* The fee is *clearly described as a Bolt-specific “platform/service fee”*, separate from the regulated taxi fare.
* It is *retained fully by Bolt* and invoiced separately to passengers (as per the intended setup).
* The disclaimer clarifies that this fee *is not part of the taximeter fare* and is linked to the *use of Bolt’s intermediation platform*.

Such a fee may be charged directly by Bolt to passengers as part of its information society services (subject to 24% VAT, invoiced separately).

Accordingly, you can *update the disclaimer* rather than rely only on the short category description. Suggested addition :

{quote}“A separate €1 Bolt platform fee applies for each ride to cover Bolt’s intermediation services. This fee is not part of the regulated taxi fare and will be invoiced separately by Bolt.”{quote}

Hello [~accountid:5ff3118b44065f013f974ef7] 

Regarding the amendment Coverflex is proposing in clause 5.2 of the Special Terms:

Considering that this amount can widely vary, increasing the limit established on clause 6.2 of the General T&C from a 3 month to a 12 month period can generate amounts that are excessive and highly disproportionate for Bolt, specially considering that it is expected that the monthly consumption of services will be quite elevated, taking into account that we establish different applicable service fees and rebate fees, the higher the monthly consumption under this Agreement.


For example, if there is a monthly consumption of 50k, maintaining the 3-month limit that we have by default in the T&C, our liability would be: 50k x 3 = 150k.
However, Coverflex intends to increase this from 3 to 12 months, which would give: 50k x 12 = 600k.
This is excessive for Bolt. The alternatives here are:

* Set a fixed amount - preferable
* Or establish/clarify exactly what is considered to be “the amounts that Coverflex has paid to Bolt” for the purposes of calculating this potential compensation.

* The *Team Lead* noted that some processes are unclear, "Specifically things related to couriers", and listed *Courier related topics* as needing improvement.



# *Payments and Refunds*

* *CS Agents* mentioned *Payments* and *Refunds* as topics needing scenario-based training, and mentioned "Resolving payment issues".

Statutory interest for delay (“_odsetki ustawowe za opóźnienie_”) under Article 481 of the Polish Civil Code applies. The interest is equal to the sum of the reference rate of the National Bank of Poland and 5.5 percentage points. 

* *Legal nature*

The interest is a compensation for delay in payment. 

* *Formal or contractual requirements*

No special formalities are required. However, we recommend sending a written demand for payment specifying the amount and the period from which statutory interest is calculated.

Please note that interest accrues from the day following the due date specified in the payment demand (if such a date was indicated) until the date the refunded amount is paid.

# We have added the EU stock-out date in *column Z*. A conditional format has been applied:
#* If the stock coverage is less than *5 months*, the cell is highlighted in *light yellow*.
#* If the stock-out date is earlier than the item’s *in-transit date*, the cell is highlighted in *red*.
# We have also added *in-transit items from CN to CWH* in *column AA*.
# *Update on ordering approach:*
Currently, we follow the method:
*In Stock + In Transit + In Production = Total Stock Coverage*.
If the total coverage is below *7 months*, the item is included in the order.
However, we observed that this method can overlook situations where the current in-stock quantity alone provides less than *1–2 months* of coverage, even though in-transit and in-production quantities inflate the total coverage. This may cause us to miss ordering the correct quantity *or create the possibility for the item to go out of stock*. 
Going forward, during order creation, we will also check the *current in-stock coverage* separately. If the in-stock coverage is less than *5 months*, the item will be included in the order as well.

+*BACKGROUND*+

* In Feb 2023, Bolt (PL) collaborated with 4Specialist (“4S”), under which 4S provided assistance services re driver registration. 
** This collaboration was terminated in September 2025, via a termination agreement.
*** 30 September 2025 = Terminated in relation to Driver Service Point in Warsaw.
*** 31 January 2026 = Terminated in relation to the remaining Driver Service Points.
** The termination agreement contained provisions relating to 4S employees that wanted to work for Bolt / Bolt-approved third parties after termination took effect. 
*** We agreed two lists: (1) a list of people who _could_ work for Bolt / Bolt-approved third parties ([here|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1pQJ0wacpbE2haPF3WasT00VHwVPUCRsUr7QpShgPAvo/edit?gid=0#gid=0]); and (2) everyone else cannot.
* From 1 October 2025, these services were taken over from 4S by Cognizant, the new vendor for Bolt on this project.
** Before this happened, several 4S staff members independently applied to work for Cognizant, responding to an open job posting.
* On *2 October*, someone from 4S who was still collaborating with Bolt accessed an internal file and saw the names of people who moved over to Cognizant.
** This was an operational miss - Access should have been removed earlier, but was instead removed 26 hours after the cutoff time. It has now been removed.
** 4S asked Bolt why these employees are still working with Bolt (via Cognizant). 4S has been trying to get in touch with the ex-employees to do the same. On 2 October, 4S submitted a formal Q asking which of their ex-employees are are still working on the Bolt project (via Cognizant).
* On 14 November, it also came to light that we shared “_at least_” two files with Cognizant: [here|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1pQJ0wacpbE2haPF3WasT00VHwVPUCRsUr7QpShgPAvo/edit?gid=0#gid=0] and [here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1xxr1cpliauHsWJYIERzHzLKuu8TerKZUwovHrB1SaQo/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.asd6jmbmjrij]. These docs contain the following about the list of ‘approved’ 4S employees: Names, contact info, salaries, 4S start dates and team leads.
** 4S has mentioned that some of the ex-employees were contacted by Cognizant’s contractor in Bangladesh.
** NB. Unclear if this access was _unauthorised_ - Cognizant people got access to the list in September
* On 21 November, the privacy team were looped in. This was escalated as a personal data incident on 24 November :melting_face: 

+*ANALYSIS*+

* The bottom line is that Radoslaw does not seem to understand why we have asked these questions, and so currently it remains unclear which access was unauthorised and which was not. This still needs to be confirmed.
* Two dimensions to assess:

Payouts are generated according to the rule
if midnight balance > current balance => current balance
if midnight balance < current balance => midnight balance

If they received less then the reported amount, it means there were active deductions on the account and we paid their current balance at the time. 


_Examples scenarios:_

# _Driver had 1000 EUR available on Sunday 23:59 and this amount was shown in their weekly report. Driver decided to cashout 300 EUR at 06:00am. Funds to be received on payout generation: 700 EUR._
# _Driver had 1000 EUR available on Sunday 23:59 and this amount was shown in their weekly report. Driver got cash orders early in the morning and the current driver balance is now showing as 802 EUR. Funds to be received on payout generation: 802 EUR._ 
# _Driver had 1000 EUR available on Sunday 23:59 and this amount was shown in their weekly report. Driver had new rides completed early Monday morning and the driver balance is now showing as 1245 EUR. Funds to be received on payout generation: 1000 EUR._
